## M2.1 step 5b, the round-id binding: "this round" stops meaning "whatever the page wrote"

WHY IT WAS NEEDED. The committee check landed at e43710a and was circular. The
page writes the contract, so the page writes `nodes`, so the page picks the
committee that its own advertisement then satisfies - honestly, with a real
bond, a real merkle proof and a real signature. Every check in the door passes.
What does not pass is the arithmetic: an id here is the tagged hash OF the
object, so changing one node in that list changes the round.

WHAT IS CHECKED, and it is first. `Client.at` refuses unless `roundId(contract)`
equals a 32-byte id the PLAYER supplied. Section 25.1 step 1 is "a link, QR,
copied round_id - carries nothing", and carrying nothing is exactly why it is
enough. In the page the id comes off `window.location.search`, which is the one
input in this whole path the page's own script did not write.

  a page naming its own node, everything else valid
                              "the page offered round 6f4a..., which is not the
                              round 8c11... you were given"
  on that node afterwards     /round 404 for BOTH ids, /transcript x-ticks 0,
                              zero batches. Asked, not assumed.
  no id, null, 31 bytes, a hex STRING
                              all refused: "nothing to check the page's
                              contract against". Required, not optional - a
                              player who arrived with no id has nothing to
                              check and there is no safe way to guess one.
  a matching id               the existing door still runs in full: committee
                              membership, proven endpoint, header chain,
                              advertisement signature, and a real round opens

MUTANTS, three killed: the id not compared (2 red), a missing id tolerated (1),
and the endpoint refusal moved ahead of the id refusal (1) - so the player is
told they are on the wrong round rather than given a chain complaint that
buries it.

AND ONE THAT COULD NOT BE KILLED, written down rather than counted. Moving the
`reach` CALL either side of the id check changes nothing observable, because
`reach` is pure: it sends no byte, opens no socket and touches no state. The
property that matters is not the order of two computations but that nothing
leaves the client first, and that is measured on the stranger's own node above.
The test comment was corrected to claim the thing it actually pins.

ONE READER STILL. `BLWP_ADVERT` is read in exactly one place, `$blwpDiscovery`,
used by both the gate and the door. The round id is a different input from a
different place - the address bar - and is read in `net.open` only.

## M2.1 5b - closed, and the three leftovers it does not cover

The door is three things, measured: the endpoint comes from a bond transaction
proven against a block header, a node this round's contract does not name is
refused, and a contract that does not hash to the round id in the address bar
is refused before anything is sent. Nothing in the live path talks before
`Client.at`.

These three are NOT bugs against that door and no code on this letter touches
them. They are written down so they are not rediscovered as surprises.

1. A LIMIT, not a bug. The round id is read from `location.search` when
   `net.open` runs, not at first paint, so a page that rewrote its own address
   bar first would be checked against its own rewrite. What the check buys is
   therefore precise and worth stating exactly: the id the player CAN STILL SEE
   is the one that is checked. That is not fixable from inside the client, and
   pretending otherwise would be worse than naming it.

2. WHICH OF THE SEVEN. The page chooses which named committee member receives
   the entry and the opening transcript. All seven are named by the round, so
   5b is satisfied; what is left is that one member sees it first, and that is
   LIVENESS AND PRIVACY, not standing: liveness because the one asked may be
   the one that is down, privacy because that member sees a player's inputs
   before anyone else does. It belongs with 13C's quorum receipts - at least
   five - and the gossip that spreads them, not here.

3. THE SAME SHAPE ONE LAYER UP, AND IT IS WHERE THE MONEY IS. `BLWP_ENTRY` -
   `stakeMsat`, `feeMsat`, `donationMsat`, `playerPubkey` - is still written by
   the page and bound to nothing the player supplied. The round-id bind fixed
   "which round"; nothing yet fixes "what am I paying". A LATER NAMED ITEM ON
   M2.1, deliberately not implemented now.

## M2.1 5c slice 1: the chain is asked of two providers, or there is no chain

WHERE THE CHAIN CAME FROM BEFORE. Nowhere. Measured: the only `fetch` in
`packages/*/src` was the three round/entry/transcript calls to the node, and no
source file had ever asked for a header. `reach` took `chains` as an argument
and the page supplied it, so a player's whole belief about Bitcoin was the
page's word - which is what 25.1 calls the failure with no symptom.

WHAT DECIDES, AND WHAT FETCHES, ARE SEPARATE. A provider is a FUNCTION handed
in, like `sign`, `verify` and the core are. `headersOverHttp(url)` is the only
transport, and the CALLER gives the whole URL: no host and no path is written
into `src`, because this protocol has no chain API of its own and a default
address would be one the player never chose. What a real provider's URLs look
like is a separate question and is not answered here.

THE RULES, and each is refused by name.

  fewer than two providers   refused BEFORE anyone is asked. Not because one
                             source is probably lying but because nothing it
                             says can be weighed: a short chain, and a chain
                             with a block hidden, are the same bytes.
  a chain that does not link  that source is discarded and named; the others
                             still answer
  fewer than two SURVIVE      refused, and the refusals are handed back
  most work wins              Bitcoin's rule, not a vote
  a shorter chain             CARRIED, not refused. Omission is the expected
                             case - "omission is answered by asking a second
                             one" - and refusing would stop a client every time
                             one source lagged, which is every day.
  a fork                      REFUSED rather than resolved, and the stray block
                             is named. Most work is the right rule for a node
                             holding the whole chain; here a fork means at
                             least one provider is lying or broken, and taking
                             the heavier one is guessing which.
  500, or no answer at all    counted and named, not waited for. A silent
                             provider must not stop the ones that answered.

MEASURED, real mainnet headers 499998-500000 served over local HTTP:

  three headers                240 bytes, 80 each
  work, each                   8045049515748916497043
  work, the three together      24135148547246749491129
  the two-header source        16090099031497832994086, and it loses
  tip                          00000000000000000024fb37364cbf81fd49cc2d51c09c75c35433c3a1945d04
  two agreeing providers       ok, agreed 2, refused []
  one whole and one short      ok, from 1, three headers
  a fork                       refused, "providers 0 and 1 do not agree"
  one provider alone           refused, and 0 calls went out
  2 good + 1 unlinked          ok, agreed 2, the broken one named
  1 good + 1 unlinked          refused, "only 1 of 2 providers gave a chain"
  a 500 and a silent one       ok on the other two; "no answer in 50 ms"
  120 bytes                    "not a whole number of headers"

## M2.1 5c, the hole in slice 1: the work was never checked to have been done

WHAT WAS WRONG. `chainWork` summed `workOf`, which reads the difficulty out of
bytes 72..76 - four bytes WRITTEN BY WHOEVER HANDS THE HEADER OVER. Nothing
asked whether the hash met the target it claimed. The comment in headers.js
said "forging is already impossible... the work is arithmetic over bytes nobody
can choose", and that sentence was simply wrong.

BEFORE, measured on the code at 54f41d2:

  mainnet 499998-500000, work    24135148547246749491129
  one fabricated header, work    57896044618658097711785492504343953926634992
                                 332820282019728792003956564819968

Thirty-two orders of magnitude, from four bytes and no mining at all.

The fork rule masked it in the obvious case - the fake chain won on work, the
honest blocks were not in it, refused - but that is a denial of service, not a
defence: one provider could make every client refuse forever. And it did NOT
mask the real attack. A provider serving the HONEST chain plus one header of
his own on the end is a SUPERSET, so every honest provider's blocks are in his,
there is no stray and nothing disagrees:

  accepted: true, from provider 1, headers 4
  winning tip   803e37e66daab4b5025b2a4231d43b46232af6396b4506aae8c8f9a453ba163a
  merkle root   bbbbbbbb...bbbbbbbb, his to choose

That merkle root is exactly what slice 2's bond proof would have been checked
against.

AFTER, the same header and the same claimed work:

  fabricated header hash        803e37e66daab4b5025b2a4231d43b46232af6396b45...
  meets its claimed target      false
  claimed work of his chain     578960446186580977117854925043439539266349923
                                32820282043863940551203314311097
  honest work                   24135148547246749491129
  two providers (one his)       refused: "only 1 of 2 providers gave a chain",
                                and provider 1 is named "this header was not
                                mined: its hash does not meet the target it
                                claims"
  three providers (two honest)  ok, agreed 2, headers 3 - his chain is
                                discarded, not obeyed, and the fabricated
                                header is not in the answer

WHAT LANDED. `targetOf` and `meetsTarget` in `protocol/src/chain.js`, and
`chainWork` refuses a header that does not meet its target BEFORE adding its
work. The byte order is the usual trap and is now written down: a block hash is
stored reversed from the way it is read as a number, so the comparison is
against the reversed bytes. A mantissa with its high bit set is a negative
target and is no target at all.

REAL HEADERS PROVE IT IS NOT JUST REFUSING EVERYTHING: mainnet 100000 and
500000 both meet their targets, and the three-header chain still weighs
24135148547246749491129.

THE FIXTURES NOW MINE. `blockOf` grinds the nonce until the hash meets the
target, because a fixture that could not be refused measures nothing. The
default bits are 0x207fffff - a target just under 2^255, so roughly every
second nonce works - since mining at mainnet difficulty in a test is not
possible. Nothing else in the suites had to change: 101 -> 104 protocol and
44 -> 46 client, with every existing fork and agreement test untouched.

MUTANTS, four, all red: the hash not compared to the target (2 protocol +
2 client), an unmined header still counted (2 + 2), a negative target treated
as a target (1), and the hash compared in display order rather than as a
number (3 + 7).

STILL ON THIS LETTER, not parked and not slice 2: the question needs a range,
so two honest providers serving different ranges are not read as a fork; one
origin counted twice must not read as two sources; the HTTP body needs a bound;
and a timed-out fetch should abort its socket.

A LIMIT, named. There is no network minimum difficulty here, so a chain of very
easy headers is accepted - it simply carries almost no work and cannot outweigh
a real chain. Enforcing a minimum, and the retarget schedule with it, is a
network-parameter decision and sits with checkpoint-or-genesis.

TESTS. protocol 101 -> 104, blwp-client 44 -> 46, blwp-node 41/41, core 85/85.
Determinism guard 19 clean, money guard 9 clean. No test-vector file changed.
No C#, no Unity, nothing deployed.

## M2.1 5c, the four leftovers on the same letter

ONE SERVER LISTED TWICE WAS TWO SOURCES, and the old test said so as if it were
a feature: `agreedChain([only.get, only.get])` answered ok, agreed 2, from one
machine. That is the worst kind of wrong - it looks exactly like the thing it
is not. `httpProvider(url)` now tags a provider with its origin and a repeated
tag is refused BEFORE anyone is asked: "providers 0 and 1 are the same source,
http://127.0.0.1:NNNNN", 0 calls out. Independence itself is NOT checkable -
two hostnames can be one machine and nothing in a client can tell - so this
catches a mistake and proves nothing, and an untagged provider is counted as
distinct because there is nothing else to do with it. Both halves are tests.

DIFFERENT RANGES WERE READ AS A FORK. Two honest providers whose answers share
no block were refused with the word used for a provider that is lying. They are
told apart now: "answered about different parts of the chain and share no
block, so neither can be weighed against the other". Still no answer - nothing
was weighed - but a different fact, and the caller is told which. The question
is also handed to the provider now (`agreedChain(providers, { ask })`), so an
honest pair CAN be asked the same thing; what a provider does with the ask is
the caller's business, and `httpProvider` takes a function of it for a provider
whose URL carries the range.

THE BODY IS BOUNDED, in both shapes a provider can send it, and the two are
different refusals on purpose:

  content-length declared    "the provider offered 320080 bytes, more than the
                             320000 this client reads" - before a byte of body
                             is pulled off the wire
  chunked, no length         "the provider sent more than the 320000 bytes this
                             client reads" - counted while reading, because
                             that header is the provider's word like the rest
  under the cap              4001 headers read, both ways

THE READ IS ABORTED, not abandoned. A provider that sends headers and then
never finishes the body used to keep a socket for the rest of the run; the
timeout now aborts it and the server sees the request aborted.

MUTANTS, six, all red: one server twice counted as two (1), disjoint ranges
read as a fork (1), the streaming cap removed (1), content-length taken at its
word (1), the abort removed (1), the question not passed on (1).

TWO THINGS THE MUTANTS TAUGHT, both about the tests rather than the code.
The content-length mutant survived at first because the streaming cap catches
it anyway - the verdict was identical, only the WORDS differed - so the test
now asserts each message against the transfer shape that produces it. And the
abort mutant made the suite HANG rather than fail, because the test left a
socket open: a hang is not a measurement, it is a test that cannot report, so
the fixture destroys its connections rather than only closing the server.

## M2.1 5c slice 2: the bond is proven into a block somebody mined

WHAT WAS LEFT. 25.1's third line - "verify: proof against header,
H(advertisement) against the bond output's commitment". The second half has
been true since the endpoint stopped coming off the page. The first half was
only ever as good as the header it was checked against, and `reach` weighed
whatever list of chains its caller handed over: mined since 969370c, but never
AGREED.

THE ATTACK, END TO END, on the same fabricated header as the last cut. He does
not need to break a hash. He needs a block whose merkle root is the one his own
proof rebuilds, and he can simply write it down:

  his block hash    6fe1215659d8493cbee898bfb8738ae75c8efdb61d7364b07092b6f8c97e499f
  his merkle root   897e0cc60ac26b827f221353a7ef2f552393f454fbfd61198eff537fff1a368f
  does his proof rebuild it?   TRUE - the merkle arithmetic passes completely
  was his block mined?         false
  provenBond                   "that is not a mined chain: this header was not
                               mined: its hash does not meet the target it
                               claims"

Before the target was checked, that same block proved his bond and his endpoint.
Hanging it off an honest block does not help either: a chain carrying it is not
a chain.

WHAT LANDED. `blwp-client/src/bond.js`. `provenBond({chain, transaction, branch,
position})` re-checks the chain rather than taking it on the caller's word - one
pass over headers already in hand, and the difference between "a block" and "80
bytes somebody handed me" - computes the txid from the transaction, and finds
the block the proof lands in. `reach` now takes `chain`, the chain two
providers already agreed on, as well as the old `chains` list, and re-checks
either.

ONE PROVIDER IS ENOUGH HERE, AND TWO ARE NEEDED FOR HEADERS. Not a preference
and worth saying plainly: the weight of a chain means nothing except in
comparison, so headers need agreement; a bond proof carries its own proof and
cannot be forged at any price, so the only lie available is silence - and
"omission is answered by asking a second one" is a search, not a vote.
`askForBond` asks in turn, keeps every refusal, and stops at the first proof.

MEASURED:

  an honest bond            proven into the mined block, header = chain[1]
  the fabricated block      refused, alone and hung off an honest one
  the right proof, position 1   "is not proven into any block of that chain"
  a chain that does not hold it refused
  bytes that are not a transaction  "not a transaction"
  three providers, two useless  proven by provider 2, both refusals kept
  a silent provider         "no answer in 50 ms", not waited for
  over real HTTP            proven, block hash matches chain[1]
  the door with an agreed chain ok, endpoint read
  the door with his block   "not a mined chain"

FIVE MUTANTS, all red: the chain taken on the caller's word (1), the proof not
checked against the header (4), the txid taken from the caller rather than
hashed (4), a refusing provider ending the search (1), an agreed chain not
re-checked in the door (1).

THE ENVELOPE IS THE TEST'S, NOT THE CLIENT'S. A bond provider is a function,
like a header provider is: the shape a chain API puts a merkle proof in is
nobody's standard, and writing one API's field names into the client would be
adopting a second protocol without saying so. The test speaks one over local
HTTP; mapping a real API onto it is not done.

NOT WIRED, and bond.js is deliberately not in the bundle: the live path still
takes `chains` from the page. Wiring is the next thing on this letter.

THE REMAINING HOLE, named and NOT opened: `agreedChain` weighs only the chains
it is handed, and nothing anchors the winner to Bitcoin. A client whose whole
provider list belongs to one operator - two hostnames, one machine, which the
origin tag catches only when it is obvious - accepts a cheaply mined chain
because there is nothing heavier to compare it with. That is
checkpoint-or-genesis, and it accounts for essentially all of what is still
missing.

## M2.1 5c slice 3: the winner has to be Bitcoin's chain, not a chain

WHAT AGREEMENT AND MINING DID NOT BUY. Together they prove only that a set of
headers is a chain of SOMETHING. Mining a short chain at trivial difficulty
costs almost nothing, so a client whose whole provider list belongs to one
operator - two hostnames, one machine, which the origin tag catches only when
it is obvious - took that operator's fork by default: there was nothing heavier
to weigh it against.

THE ANCHOR IS REQUIRED AND MAY NOT COME FROM THE PAGE. An anchor an attacker
supplies is no anchor, because he would name a block of his own fork. It is a
caller's argument, brought by the client.

  no anchor                 refused, and this is the measured "before": two
                            providers agreeing perfectly on a four-header
                            chain he mined himself, every header meeting its
                            target, and nothing to refuse him with
  his chain, with an anchor  "only 0 of 2 providers gave a chain", both named
                            "this chain does not contain ..., the block this
                            client is anchored to". It is not weighed at all -
                            it is an answer to a different question.
  the honest chain          accepted, 3 headers, work 24135148547246749491129
  the fabricated header     still refused, unchanged from 969370c

`BITCOIN_MAINNET_GENESIS` is in `protocol/src/chain.js`, hashing order, and the
test checks it displays as
000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f. It is not a
parameter and not a choice: that number IS mainnet, anyone can check it, it
cannot go stale, and no operator can change it.

THE SPEC'S OWN NUMBER IS WRONG, and it decides checkpoint-vs-genesis. 25.1 says
"80 bytes a block; under 4 MB for all of history". Measured: 500,000 headers is
38.1 MB, 800,000 is 61.0 MB, 900,000 is 68.7 MB - seventeen times the figure in
the spec. No browser will fetch that to open a round, so a deployment will
anchor on a later block instead, which is a constant somebody must choose and
keep fresh. WHICH block is not decided here; that there must be one is.

A BRANCH DELETED RATHER THAN LEFT UNREACHABLE. The "answers about different
parts of the chain" refusal from the last cut cannot happen any more: every
chain that gets weighed contains the anchor, so any two of them share at least
that block. Keeping it would have been a branch no test and no mutant could
reach. The same fact is said earlier now, per source, by name.

MUTANTS, four, all red: the anchor made optional (2), a chain not required to
contain it (2), the anchor checked only on the winner rather than per source
(2), and the genesis constant changed by one byte (1).

WHAT SHARE THIS CLOSES. The chain source had one hole left after headers, PoW
and the bond, and this is it: the anchor accounts for essentially all of the
remaining chain-source gap. What is left is not the chain source.

LEFTOVERS OF THIS SLICE, not a new letter: the merkle-proof envelope is still
the test's rather than a real API's; `bond.js` is not in the bundle; the live
path still takes `chains` from the page, so the door is not yet fed by
`agreedChain`; and which block a deployment anchors on - genesis at 68.7 MB or
a shipped checkpoint that must be kept fresh - is a constant nobody has chosen.

## M2.1 5c slice 4: the door asks for the chain instead of being handed one

WHAT WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS THE WHOLE POINT OF 5C. Everything measured in the
four cuts before this was a library nothing used. Grepped, not remembered:
neither `client.js` nor `directory.js` nor the jslib called `agreedChain`,
`askForBond` or `provenBond`, and the jslib handed `transaction`, `branch` and
`chains` straight off `BLWP_ADVERT`. `reach` verified whatever it was given -
which proves a chain and a proof agree WITH EACH OTHER and nothing whatever
about Bitcoin, because a page that wrote both wrote a consistent pair. 25.1 is
normative about what a CLIENT does, so until the door asks, the chain source
was not the client's chain source.

WHAT LANDED. `discover()` in `directory.js`: two provider functions for
headers, weighed and anchored; then bond providers asked in turn until one
proves a bond into that chain; then the endpoint read out of it. `Client.at`
calls it, and REFUSES a ready-made chain or proof rather than verifying one -
`chain`, `chains`, `transaction`, `branch` and `position` are each named:
"must come from a provider, not from whoever opened the page: two things that
agree with each other are not Bitcoin".

MEASURED THROUGH THE DOOR, not through the library:

  a perfect bundle handed over    reach(raw) accepts it - said out loud in the
                                  test so the refusal cannot be mistaken for
                                  the bundle being bad - and Client.at refuses
                                  all five keys by name
  the same bytes, asked for       the round opens, base https://node.example:443
  one provider                    "no chain: 1 providers is fewer than the 2"
  no anchor                       "no chain: no anchor"
  an anchor the chain lacks       "no chain: only 0 of 2 providers gave a chain"
  no bond provider                "no bond: no providers to ask for the bond"
  a proof landing nowhere         "no bond: no provider proved that bond into
                                  the chain" - provenBond, on the live path
  the attacker's whole world      his own mined chain, his own bond in it, his
                                  own signed advertisement, served by two
                                  providers that agree completely: accepted
                                  when anchored on his own first block, and
                                  "only 0 of 2 providers gave a chain" when
                                  anchored on a block this client knows

THE CLIENT SPEAKS BITCOIN'S SHAPES AND NOBODY'S JSON: 80-byte headers back to
back, and a merkle branch of 32-byte hashes with an index. No explorer schema
and no host or path is in the package. Translating a real API into these
functions is an adapter that lives on the page or the node, where it can be
changed without touching anything that decides.

THE JSLIB. `$blwpDiscovery` now reads `BLWP_CHAIN.headers`, `.bonds` and
`.anchor` and REFUSES a page still carrying `chains`, `chain`, `transaction` or
`branch` - a page on the old path is told so rather than quietly taken at its
word. It also refuses fewer than two header providers, no bond provider, and a
missing anchor, each by name.

`BlwpNetNodeUrl` can no longer answer with an address: the address is now read
off a bond proven into a chain two providers agreed on, and every step of that
is a fetch. What C# does with the answer is ask whether it is empty, so it
answers whether a session is worth opening - "the chain", or empty for none -
and the address is resolved in `net.open`, before a byte is sent. Renaming the
C# side is C# and was out of scope.

`bond.js` and `headers.js` are in the bundle now, which follows from the import
rather than being arranged: 15 modules -> 17, 102.9 KB -> 120.3 KB.

MUTANTS, five red: a handed chain verified rather than refused (1), the agreed
chain not the one `reach` checks (7), a refused chain still opening a session
(2), a refused bond still opening one (1), the bond's position not carried
through (7). A sixth was written badly - `bond.branch = bond.branch` changes
nothing - and is not counted.

ONE TEST FIXTURE FAULT FOUND AND FIXED, not a rule loosened: two tests said
`reach({ ...fixture, chains: X })` while the fixture had grown a `chain` key,
which takes precedence, so the override was silently ignored. They now offer
the chain they mean to.

## M2.1 5c slice 5: the client brings the anchor, and a page that offers one is refused

THE HOLE, AND IT WAS MINE. dd18cca wired the door to providers and then took
the anchor off `BLWP_CHAIN`. `directory.js` said, in a comment I had written
myself, "It is a caller's argument rather than a page's value on purpose. An
anchor an attacker supplies is no anchor - he would name a block of his own
fork"; the jslib said "The anchor is the page's to CARRY" and did exactly what
the first comment forbids. Weighing, mining and the bond proof were all honest,
and the block they were all anchored TO arrived from the page.

So the headline of that cut did not hold on the live path. The attacker's world
was refused only when anchored on a block the client knew, and through the
jslib he supplied that too.

WHAT LANDED. `discover` anchors on `BITCOIN_MAINNET_GENESIS`, always, and a
supplied `anchor` is refused by name rather than used - the same shape as the
five handed keys: "the anchor is the client's own and may not be supplied: a
block chosen by whoever handed over the chain is not a block the client knows".
The jslib no longer reads `BLWP_CHAIN.anchor` and the comment that said it
should is gone.

`BITCOIN_MAINNET_GENESIS_HEADER` - the eighty bytes, not only the hash - is in
`protocol/src/chain.js` so a chain can START at Bitcoin's first block. Nothing
about it is taken on trust: the test hashes it and gets
000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f, and that is
the only reason to believe either the header or the hash constant beside it.
The fixtures were rebuilt on it, so an honest chain contains the block the
client knows because it IS that block, not because a fixture said so.

MEASURED THROUGH THE LIVE SHAPE:

  his whole world, every field a page can give
      his own mined first block, his bond in the next, his signed
      advertisement for a node on this round's committee, two providers
      agreeing completely
    the library, handed his chain      ACCEPTS it - asserted, so the refusal
                                       cannot be mistaken for a bad bundle
    the door                           "no chain: only 0 of 2 providers gave a
                                       chain" - his chain does not contain
                                       genesis
    him offering his own anchor        "the anchor is the client's own and may
                                       not be supplied"
  an honest chain rooted at genesis    opens, base https://node.example:443
  genesis header                       hashes to the block everybody knows;
                                       80 bytes; matches the hash constant

MUTANTS. Two red: a page-supplied anchor used rather than refused (2), the
genesis header changed by one byte (9). A third - adding `anchor ||` in front
of the constant - killed nothing and is NOT counted: the guard above refuses a
supplied anchor first, so the fallback is unreachable and the mutation changes
nothing observable. Same shape as the reach-ordering non-mutant recorded
earlier.

## M2.1 5c slice 6: the two-provider floor is the client's, not a page setting

THE HOLE, FOUND BY WALKING THE DOOR PATH AGAINST THE LIBRARY PATH. `discover`
took `least` and `timeoutMs` from its caller, and `Client.at` spreads the
page's own object into it. Measured through `Client.at` before the fix, on a
chain honestly rooted at genesis:

  least default, ONE provider   refused: "1 providers is fewer than the 2 it
                                takes to weigh one against another"
  page sets least: 1            https://one-provider.example:443   -- OPENS

So the first clause of 5c's goal - "asks two providers" - was not true on the
live path: one field turned "several independent sources, most work wins" into
one source, and a short chain and a chain with a block hidden are the same
bytes. It is the same fault as the anchor, in the same function, and I did not
catch it while fixing the anchor.

WHAT LANDED. `PROVIDERS_NEEDED = 2` and `PROVIDER_WAIT_MS = 10000` are named
constants in `directory.js`, and `discover` refuses a supplied `least` or
`timeoutMs` by name - the same shape as the anchor and the five handed keys:
"least is the client's own and may not be supplied: how many providers must
agree, and how long to wait for them, are not settings for whoever handed over
the providers".

`ask` is deliberately NOT refused. It names which range of chain to fetch, and
a lie about it can only omit - which is the one lie a second provider answers.
A test asserts it still reaches both header providers and the bond provider.

MEASURED THROUGH `Client.at`:

  one provider, nothing supplied     "no chain: 1 providers is fewer than the 2"
  least: 1, one provider             "least is the client's own and may not be
                                     supplied"
  least: 1 with two providers        same refusal - it is refused for being
                                     offered, not for the number
  least: 5                           same refusal
  timeoutMs 0, 1, 60000, 999999999   "timeoutMs is the client's own and may not
                                     be supplied", each one
  nothing of the client's supplied   opens, base https://node.example:443
  ask: { from: 0, count: 2 }         reaches both header providers and the bond
                                     provider, unchanged

MUTANTS, four, all red: a supplied `least` used (1), a supplied `timeoutMs`
used (1), the floor lowered to one (2), the floor not passed to `agreedChain`

## M2.1 5c slice 7: two providers means two sources, not two calls

THE HOLE. The origin tag existed and only `httpProvider` set it, so it never
fired where it matters. On the live path the PAGE writes the provider
functions, and they carry nothing:

  two untagged providers, same function   tag is undefined

so `[f, f]` - one server, listed twice - counted as two sources and the
two-provider floor counted CALLS. Same shape as `least`: a rule that held in
the library and never fired at the door.

WHAT LANDED. `discover` refuses a provider that does not declare a source, and
refuses two that declare the same one, before anyone is asked. Header and bond
providers are one class with one rule; splitting them would have been a second
kind of provider with quieter rules.

  two raw functions           "header provider 0 does not say which source it
                              is: a provider must carry a tag, or two calls to
                              one server count as two sources"
  one tagged, one not         "header provider 1 does not say which source it is"
  two with the same tag       "header providers 0 and 1 are the same source,
                              one.example: one server listed twice is not two"
  an untagged bond provider   "bond provider 0 does not say which source it is"
  two distinct tags           two providers, and the round opens on
                              https://node.example:443

THE LIMIT, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED AWAY, because writing "independence is
not checkable" into this file and closing would have made "two providers" mean
"two calls":

  one server behind two names   accepted, and `calls` counts 2 - one machine
                                answered twice and the client could not tell

There is nothing to read. Two honest providers on the same chain return the
same bytes, so agreement is exactly what an honest pair looks like, and a
browser has no network identity to check a name against. A tag is a
DECLARATION, not a proof. What it buys is that the obvious case is refused and
that a lie has to be written down as a lie instead of being the default.

MUTANTS, three, all red: an untagged provider accepted (1), the same tag twice
treated as two sources (1), only header providers required to declare (1).

ONE FIXTURE FIXED, not a rule loosened: the lying bond provider in "the door
will not open on one provider" was untagged and started failing for the tag
instead of the proof. It now declares a source, so the claim it makes -
`provenBond` runs on the live path - is the claim it tests.

## M2.1 step 3, quorum: a mark is live at five receipts, not at one

WHAT THE CLIENT DID BEFORE, read out of the code rather than guessed:

  0 receipts   the head does not move - readReceipt throws first
  1 receipt    this.head = markId
  4            identical to 1
  5            identical to 1
  7            identical to 1

A step function at ONE, where 13C puts the threshold at five. There was no
count and no threshold anywhere in `blwp-client/src`; the only counter in the
repo was `receiptCount` on the node, whose own comment says whether five is
enough needs the other six daemons. So "the head moves on a verified receipt,
not on a word" was true and thinner than it sounded: one receipt out of seven.

WHAT LANDED. `RECEIPTS_FOR_LIVE = 5`, a `witnesses` map of mark id -> the SET
of distinct committee keys that have receipted it, `witnessed(markId)` and
`live(markId)`, and the head advancing only on live. Receipts recovered after
a reconnect count towards the same total.

MEASURED, with the node's own key plus six real Ed25519 committee keys signing
real CheckpointReceipts through the same door a gossiped one arrives by:

  0 sent        head at NO_PREVIOUS, nothing witnessed
  1 (the node)  witnessed 1, live false, head unmoved
  4             witnessed 4, live false, head unmoved
  5             witnessed 5, live TRUE, head = the mark
  7             witnessed 7, live true, still the same one head
  one signer five times      witnessed 2, not 6 - 13C counts NODES
  a stranger's receipt       refused, "is not on this round's committee"
  a committee key claimed,
    signed by somebody else  refused, "does not verify under its own key"
  an honest receipt for
    another mark             refused, "the receipt is for ..."
  after all three refusals   witnessed still 2, head still NO_PREVIOUS

## M2.1 13C: the equivocation proof, the one part one node can hold up alone

THE FRACTION, MEASURED BEFORE THE WORK. Sections 13, 13A and 13C name six
artefacts. Two now exist: the receipt with its counting, and the canonical

and slashing appear NOWHERE.

The no-quorum rule is three clauses, and they do not cost the same:

  1. FORFEIT if the disagreement is explained by PROVEN player equivocation
     (13B). Needs two signed checkpoints and the session key. No committee, no
     replay, no core.
  2. otherwise VOID, the stake refunded by letting the HTLC expire, the entry
     excluded from the pool and the payout table. Needs a RESULT with 5-of-7
     signatures, the result window, and Lightning.
  3. nodes whose signature contradicts a replay are slashed. Needs the bond
     output of 5A.3B - MuSig2, an arbitration quorum, `bond_maturity` - and a
     replay to contradict.

So of the four artefacts still missing, ONE does not need a committee, and it
is the one the other two clauses are conditioned on: clause 2 begins
"Otherwise", so without clause 1 it cannot even be evaluated. That is this cut.
Clauses 2 and 3 are the remaining three of four and every one of them needs
either the other six daemons or the bond on chain.

## M2.1 13C: equivocation forfeits, disagreement without a proof is VOID

THE RULE, and its asymmetry is the whole of it: "a player cannot manufacture a
refund by causing disagreement, because the only way a player can cause it is
equivocation, and equivocation forfeits. Everything else that goes wrong is the
infrastructure's fault and refunds."

`noQuorumOutcome({ signatures, needed, equivocationProven })` in
`protocol/src/payout.js`. Both inputs were already in the tree - the fork proof
a node publishes, and a count of committee signatures - and the output is the
word `computePayoutTable` has consumed since before this slice. No daemon is
invented and none is pretended at.

MEASURED on one node, with the evidence taken off the doors exactly as a
stranger takes it - GET /equivocation, then GET /entry for the session key,
then `provesEquivocation`:

  A, signed two chains, 3 of 5    FORFEIT: "no quorum at 3 of 5, and the player
                                  signed two chains: 13B forfeits the entry"
  B, played straight, 3 of 5      VOID: "nothing shows the player caused it"
  the fork proof off the door     A true, B false - a straight player is not
                                  proven a forker
  5 of 5                          outcome null, "the committee agreed" - this
                                  rule says it does not apply rather than
                                  guessing

AND THE ASYMMETRY IN MONEY, which is where it has to be true:

  DELIVERED + FORFEIT + VOID   pool 100000 msat - the forfeited stake and
                               nothing else
                               table 2 rows: the void entry is not in it at all
                               winner 200000 msat: own stake plus the forfeited
  the same round with the
    forker VOIDed instead      pool 0, winner 100000 - only the stake back

So a player who could VOID by causing disagreement would have a free refund on
every losing round, and that is exactly the door 13C closes.

ONLY `true` FORFEITS. undefined, null, 'yes', 1, {} and an unawaited Promise
all give VOID. A truthy check would forfeit a stake on a Promise somebody
forgot to await, which is a stake taken by a typo. A count that is not a count
is refused rather than guessed: negative, fractional, or a threshold of zero.

PLAYER_LOST WAS NOT INVENTED. FORFEIT already names the case where the player's
own conduct costs the stake, and a synonym would be a second word for one
outcome and a second place to get it wrong.

THE PROOF IS TAKEN AS ALREADY CHECKED, deliberately: `provesEquivocation` needs
a curve, `packages/protocol` carries none, and a decision that re-verified
would need one. The caller passes what it has verified, and the test verifies
it the way a third party would rather than trusting the node that served it.

MUTANTS, four, all red: a fork not forfeiting so everything voids (1), anything
truthy forfeiting (1), no quorum never noticed so the rule never applies (2), a
short committee counted as agreement (2).

## M2.1 13C: a VOID stake goes back, and the operator takes nothing

WHAT THE HOLD PATH DID BEFORE. Nothing. `stakeCommitment` is H(P), the
hold-invoice preimage commitment, carried in the entry contract, and `funded`
is a predicate the operator supplies. Grepped across `packages/*/src`: no
settle, no cancel, no preimage release, no refund - the words appear only in
comments. So on VOID, on FORFEIT and on a delivered win the hold did the same
thing, which was nothing, and a stake nobody decides about is a stake the
operator is holding.

Of 13C clause 2's three parts - the decision, the exclusion from pool and
table, the refund by HTLC expiry - two were in (the decision at 7775643, the
exclusion since before this letter) and this is the third.

WHAT LANDED. `holdSettlement({ roundId, entries, minScore })` in
`protocol/src/payout.js`. Every entry gets exactly one of two answers, because
a hold invoice has exactly two: SETTLE, release the preimage and take it, or
CANCEL, let it expire back to the payer.

  VOID            CANCEL - the fault was the operator's, so the operator takes
                  nothing
  anything else   SETTLE - the stake joins the pot the payout table shares out

MEASURED, before and after, msat:

  DELIVERED-100 + FORFEIT + VOID
    settled 200000, refunded 100000, paid 200000, rows 2, winner 200000
    the void stake is in no row, and settled == paid exactly
  DELIVERED-100 + FORFEIT (no void)
    settled 200000, refunded 0, winner 200000 - a forfeited stake is SPENT.
    Refunding it would hand a player who signed two chains their money back
    and leave the winner nothing to be paid from.
  DELIVERED + FORFEIT + VOID + VOID
    settled + refunded 400000 - no stake goes missing; refunded 200000
  everyone VOID
    settled 0, paid 0, refunded 300000, and the table has no rows at all -
    the case an operator would most like to be paid for

A HOLE IN THE PAYOUT MODEL, found by probing the table rather than reading it.
`computePayoutTable` says a cautious player "keeps their stake and simply does
not place" - and gives them ZERO while their hold, not being VOID, settles.
Zero paid and a stake taken is the operator keeping it. With no loser in the
round the pool is empty and the table's own invariant is skipped, so nothing
caught it. `holdSettlement` refuses: "the operator would keep 100000 msat:
settled 200000 against 100000 paid out". It is refused rather than quietly
paid, and the payout model is where the fix belongs - named here, not silently
patched.

## M2.1 13C: the cautious player keeps their stake, and the table says who settles

WHAT WAS WRONG. `computePayoutTable` has always carried the sentence "a
cautious player keeps their stake and simply does not place", and then paid
that player ZERO while their hold - not being VOID - settled. Zero paid and a
stake taken is the operator keeping it. With no loser in the round the pool is
empty and the table's own invariant was skipped, so nothing noticed.
`holdSettlement` refusing that input was a detector, not the fix.

WHAT LANDED. The table now names WHICH stakes enter the pot and returns that
set; a delivered player below the score is not among them. `holdSettlement`
reads that set rather than deciding again - two places deciding which stakes
move is two places to get it wrong - and the balance check no longer waits for
a non-empty pool, because an empty one was exactly where the money went
missing.

MEASURED, msat, all five fixtures:

  fixture                     settled  refunded    paid  rows  winner  operator
  DELIVERED+FORFEIT+VOID       200000    100000  200000     2  200000         0
  DELIVERED+FORFEIT            200000         0  200000     2  200000         0
  everyone VOID                     0    300000       0     0       0         0
  bold+cautious, minScore 50   100000    100000  100000     2  100000         0
  bold+cautious+FAILED         200000    100000  200000     3  200000         0

Before, the fourth row could not be answered at all - `holdSettlement` refused
it, and the table alone would have paid the winner 100000 while 100000 of the
cautious player's money sat settled with nobody. The operator column is zero on
every row, and that is the property.

A ROUND NOBODY FINISHED. Everybody FAILED: the pool holds every stake and there
is no qualifier to hand it to. The table answers without complaint, because its
own invariant only applies when somebody qualified, so the only thing between
the operator and the whole pot is this equality - "the operator would keep
200000 msat: settled 200000 against 0 paid out". What such a round should do
with the pot is a decision nobody has made; refusing is not that decision, it
is declining to pay it to the house by default. One finisher and it answers:
settled 300000, paid 300000, the finisher taking 300000.

MUTANTS, five. Red: the cautious stake put back into the pot (2), holdSettlement
deciding for itself instead of reading the table (2), a VOID hold settled to the
operator (5), and the balance check removed (1). The balance check was 0 red
against the fixed table until the no-finisher input existed - every other
fixture balances by construction now - which is why that test was written
rather than the check dropped.

## M2.1 13C payout table: every outcome combination, probed

Not reasoned about - run. `settled + refunded == every stake` is the
"accounted" column, and the operator column is what the house would keep:

  FAILED only                     REFUSED: "would keep 200000 msat"
  FAILED + VOID, no qualifier     REFUSED: "would keep 100000 msat"
  FORFEIT only                    REFUSED: "would keep 100000 msat"
  FAILED + below-score DELIVERED  REFUSED: "would keep 100000 msat"
  below-score DELIVERED only      settled 0, refunded 100000, operator 0, accounted
  two DELIVERED, both qualify     settled 200000, refunded 0, paid 200000, operator 0
  VOID only                       settled 0, refunded 200000, operator 0, accounted
  no entries at all               all zero, accounted
  one DELIVERED, zero stake       all zero, accounted

So a pool with no qualifier is refused in every shape it comes in, and every
shape that answers has the operator at zero with every stake accounted for.

THE GUARD CANNOT BE WRONGLY SKIPPED, which is the one thing worth checking
about `if (activated.length && settledMsat !== paidMsat)`: a mismatch needs a
SETTLING entry, and a settling entry is an activated one, so there is no input
where money moves and the check is skipped. `holdSettlement` recomputing
`activated` for that length is a second computation of the word but not a
second decision about pot membership - the pot is `table.settling` and nothing
else reads anything else.

WHAT REMAINS OF 13/13A/13C, and it is 5 pieces: the result window that says
when to ask, `PlayerResult` with 5-of-7 on a result and PROVISIONALLY_FINAL,
the objection window, slashing, and the Lightning that actually settles or
cancels an invoice. FOUR are protocol rules and ONE is operator plumbing. Of
the four rules, three need the committee to exist; the exception is the
`PlayerResult` OBJECT and its signature, which can be built on one node exactly
as `CheckpointReceipt` was built before anything issued one.

signed THE SAME one. Not the replay that produces it, not the objection window,
not a live committee. The same order `CheckpointReceipt` was built in: the
object first, issuing it later, said out loud rather than passed off as done.

## M2.1 13: nobody is on a committee by signing something

THE HOLE IN 0f3c4a0, found by probing the function rather than re-reading the

  five keys on NO committee, same bytes
    -> {"final":true,"signers":5,"why":"5 of 5 signed the same result:

  five members + one stranger   final TRUE, signers 5, strangers 1 - one stray

  four members                  not final
  five members                  PROVISIONALLY_FINAL
  one member five times         1 signer
  3/4 split at seven signatures not final, strongest side 4

A SIGNED-OBJECT FORMAT CHANGE, made once. The round contract gained

minutes, CONTRACT-DEFINED" and a window the caller chooses is a window the
operator chooses - the operator being the party a veto exists against. The
player signs up to it with the rest of the round. `OBJECTION_WINDOW_REFERENCE_MS
= 600000n` is a REFERENCE and not a default: the number lives in the contract.

                        is the one the change is in

TWO THINGS THE SPEC SAYS THAT THE ASK HAD BACKWARDS, and both are in the code
now rather than in a comment:

  WHO MAY OBJECT IS ANYONE. "the affected player, another player in the round,

  A VALID OBJECTION DOES NOT VOID. "A valid objection suspends finality. The

## M2.1 13A: the two ways a claim could still stop a paid round

BOTH FOUND BY PROBING `finality` AND `objectionHolds` AGAINST EACH OTHER, which
is what the six mutants on the cut before had not done: each property was
measured on its own and nothing crossed them.

  probe 1, before   an objection dated 999999 ms past the close: holds true,
                    finality SUSPENDED - a settled round un-finalised by
                    anybody who could produce one valid objection
  probe 1, after    holds true (the objection is sound, only late) ->
                    state FINAL, late 1, "came too late to reopen it"

  probe 2, before   an objection naming ANOTHER round and another result:
                    holds true, finality SUSPENDED - every check that existed
                    passed, because they were checks about a different round
  probe 2, after    holds false, "that objection is about round 7777...",
                    and the state stays PROVISIONALLY_FINAL

WHAT CHANGED. `objectionHolds` now requires the round and result being
finalised and refuses without them - a caller that does not say what is being
objected to cannot be told whether the objection is about it. `finality` works
out the window FIRST and only then looks for an objection, and an objection
counts only if ITS OWN timestamp fell inside the window: at or after the result
went provisional, and strictly before the close. 13A opens the window after
PROVISIONALLY_FINAL; 14 says once FINAL, later failure does not erase it.

  atMs = closes            FINAL, late 1 - the same boundary the state uses

  atMs before the round went provisional   ignored, PROVISIONALLY_FINAL
  another round / another result           does not hold, does not suspend
  no round or result given                 refused rather than assumed

## M2.1 13C/23.2: the HTLC path, and two action words that were wrong

WHAT THE HTLC PATH DOES TODAY, measured before anything was written: NOTHING.
The only trace of it in `packages/*/src` is `stakeCommitment` in the entry
contract - "H(P), the hold-invoice preimage commitment" - and the word
`preimage` appears twice in the whole tree, both in comments. No invoice state,
no share, no release, no cancel. So the answer to "does the HTLC path cancel
the hold, or does only the table say refund" is: ONLY THE TABLE SAYS REFUND.

AND TWO OF ITS THREE ANSWERS WERE WRONG against 23.2, which is worse than the
missing plumbing because it is the money law rather than the wiring:

  23.2                          what holdSettlement answered
  DELIVERED  Cancel the HTLC    SETTLE - the winner's stake was moved into the
             -> returns to the           pool and paid back out of it. 23.2
             player                      never moves it.
  FAILED /   Settle the HTLC    SETTLE - agreed
  FORFEIT    -> the pool wallet
  VOID       DO NOTHING; it     CANCEL - and a cancel REQUIRES 5-of-7
             expires and the             settlement signatures, so a refund
             wallet is refunded          became something an operator could
             automatically               withhold by doing nothing

"The default path - nobody acting - is always the refund. That is what makes
infrastructure failure safe." Only SETTLE may move money away from a player,
and it is the one direction with conditions on it.

WHAT LANDED. `settlementAction` answers the action AND what it still needs:

  VOID                       NOTHING, authorised with no conditions at all,
                             even from a SUSPENDED result with zero shares and
                             zero signatures
  FAILED / FORFEIT           SETTLE, and refused until: the result is FINAL,
                             at least 5 preimage shares, 5-of-7 settlement
                             signatures. Each missing one is NAMED - a bare
                             call lists three, not one.
  DELIVERED, qualifying      CANCEL, needing 5-of-7 settlement signatures
  DELIVERED, below the score CANCEL, "the stake was never at risk"

AND THE POOL IS EXACTLY THE LOSERS' STAKES. A qualifier's own stake never
enters it, so the equality is over SHARES rather than amounts: the table hands
a winner `stake + share`, and only the share half comes out of the pool.

  DELIVERED + FORFEIT + VOID   pool 100000, refunded 200000, shares 100000
  no loser at all              pool 0, refunded 200000, both CANCEL
  bold + cautious + FAILED     pool 100000, refunded 200000, shares 100000
  everyone VOID                all NOTHING, pool 0, refunded 300000, no rows
  nobody finished              refused: "the operator would keep 200000 msat:
                               a pool of 200000 against 0 handed out"

Operator take is zero in every combination that answers, and the one that
cannot answer refuses rather than defaulting in the house's favour.

MUTANTS, eight, all red: a VOID refund turned into a cancel so somebody must
act (3), a VOID refund made to wait for signatures (1), a winner's stake
settled into the pool (3), a loser settled without a FINAL result (1), without

THE TESTS WERE RESTATED, NOT LOOSENED. Every assertion in `hold.test.js`

WHAT STILL NEEDS THE OTHER SIX DAEMONS, and it is the plumbing rather than the

## M2.1 23.1: five of seven rebuild the stake preimage, four rebuild nothing

WHAT 23.4 SAYS THIS BUYS: "Settling a loser's HTLC requires reconstructing P,
which requires 5 of the 7 shares, which the mechanical rule releases only
against a FINAL result." So the property that matters is what FOUR colluding
settlement nodes hold, and it is measured rather than asserted.

THE FIELD is 2^521 - 1, a Mersenne prime anybody can check, chosen because a
32-byte preimage has to fit in one element with room to spare - reducing P into
a smaller field would change the number whose hash the player already
committed to. Exact BigInt throughout; no float near it, for the same reason
none goes near the payout table.

MEASURED, and not on a sample:

  every four of the seven      all 35 combinations refused: "4 shares cannot
                               reconstruct anything: 5 are needed"
  four interpolated anyway     the answer is NOT P - checked on five of the 35
                               by asking for a four-of-four reconstruction of
                               the same points
  every five of the seven      all 21 combinations rebuild P exactly, and
                               sha256 of what came back equals the
                               stakeCommitment the player signed
  six and seven                also rebuild P
  three, two, one, none        refused the same way
  one seat answering twice     "two shares for one seat are one share"
  a share altered in transit   fails its seat's commitment
  seat 1's value as seat 2's   fails - a member cannot hand over another's
                               share as their own and be counted twice
  a different secret, and the
  same secret with different
  randomness                   different shares, and each rebuilds its own

MUTANTS, seven, and one survived first: four shares enough (1), the threshold
set to four (6), one seat twice counted as two (1), the secret not the constant
term (2), a Lagrange term dropped (3), a share consistent with any commitment
(1), and the seat left out of the commitment - 0 red until a test presented one
seat's value under another seat's name, and 1 red after.

WHAT "VERIFIABLE" MEANS HERE, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. Each share carries a
commitment its holder can check against the share it was given, so a share
corrupted in transit or swapped by whoever passed it on is caught without
reconstructing anything - the literal reading of 23.1. It is NOT Feldman: it
does not prove the dealer used ONE polynomial for all seven seats. That needs
commitments in a group with a hard discrete log, this package carries no group
for the same reason it carries no curve, and a dishonest dealer would be caught
at reconstruction rather than at handout. Named here rather than papered over,
and it is the hole in this piece.

TESTS. protocol 125 -> 131, blwp-node 66, blwp-client 72, core 85. Money guard
9 files clean, determinism guard 19 clean. No Unity, no C#, no browser.

## M2.1 23.1: what a dishonest dealer can still do, counted

THE CONTRACT OF THIS PIECE IS SHARE-TO-SEAT BINDING, NOT POLYNOMIAL BINDING.
It is not Feldman and it is not unqualified VSS, and the module, the tests and
this file all say so. A dealer who splits with two polynomials and gives some
seats the second one hands out shares that EACH pass their own seat commitment;
nothing at handout can tell.

THE PLAYER IS THE DEALER, so this is not an operator fault: it is a player
arranging that a loss can never be settled.

COUNTED over all 21 ways to pick five of seven, with k seats given a second
polynomial's share:

  k   every share passes its seat?   subsets that open P   refused
  0   yes                            21                     0
  1   yes                             6                    15
  2   yes                             1                    20
  3   yes                             0                    21

So a player needs to mis-share THREE of their own seven to make it impossible
for any five honest settlement nodes to open the committed preimage. That is
the whole of the escape, and it is the fraction: at k=3 the honest side has 0
of 21 workable subsets while every share still looks correct to its holder.

CLOSED THIS TURN, the half that needs no group: `reconstruct` takes the
`stakeCommitment` - H(P), already in the entry contract the player signed - and
refuses an answer that does not hash to it. Measured on a k=3 handout: some
subsets produce a well-formed 32-byte value that is NOT P, and unchecked those
come back looking exactly like a preimage. With the commitment checked, all 21
refuse. `openStake` tries every subset and answers "none of the 21 ways to pick
5 shares opens the committed preimage" rather than handing back a wrong one.

A NUMBER THAT MOVED, and what was done about it: how many of the 21 land inside
32 bytes at all is LUCK - a mixed interpolation lands somewhere in a 521-bit
field - and asserting 19 directly passed once and failed the next run at 16.
The test asserts the invariant instead: the ones that do land there are wrong,
and with the commitment checked every subset is refused. Three consecutive runs
green.

NOT CLOSED, and it cannot be without a group: catching the mis-share at
HANDOUT. That is Feldman - commitments in a group with a hard discrete log -
and this package carries no group for the same reason it carries no curve.

AND A GAP IN THE SPEC ITSELF, named not invented: 13C makes VOID the operator's
fault and FORFEIT the player's. A player who mis-shares P has caused a
settlement failure by their own conduct, which reads like 13B's logic, but 13B
is about equivocation and says nothing about sharing. Nothing here decides it.

MUTANTS, four, and one was a no-op: the answer not checked against the
commitment (2), openStake trying only the first subset (1), a wrong preimage
opened when the commitment is absent (2), and openStake reporting success
without opening anything - written first as `back || new Uint8Array(32)`, which
changes nothing because `back` is always truthy, then as `ok: true`.

TESTS. protocol 131 -> 133, blwp-node 66, blwp-client 72, core 85. Money guard
9 files clean, determinism guard 19 clean. No Unity, no C#.

## M2.1 23.1: a handout nobody can open is FORFEIT, not VOID

THE CLASSIFICATION, decided by Daniel and encoded here. The player IS the
dealer of their own stake preimage - 23.1 has them split P and encrypt one
share to each settlement seat - so a handout where no five of the seven open
the committed P did not happen to anybody. It was made, and only the player
could have made it.

VOID is the operator-fault path: nobody acts, the HTLC expires, the stake goes
home. Calling a sabotaged handout VOID would hand a losing player their money
back for having broken settlement themselves, which is the same family as
escaping by disconnect.

BEFORE AND AFTER, in msat, one winner and one saboteur at 100000 each:

                     pool   refunded   winner   operator
  as FORFEIT (now)  100000    100000   200000          0
  as VOID (before)       0    200000   100000          0

So the difference is exactly the stake: as VOID the dealer has it back and the
winner is paid nothing beyond their own; as FORFEIT it pays the winner. The
house takes zero either way, which is the other half of the property - this
closes a player escape without opening an operator one.

  the saboteur's hold   SETTLE - it is not handed back
  the winner's hold     CANCEL - a winner's stake still never enters the pool
  pool - shares         0

`handoutOutcome` reads `openStake`'s answer and nothing else: a committee that
cannot open a preimage has already tried every subset, and this is not a second
judgement. An honest handout returns no outcome at all - it is nothing to do
with this rule - and anything that is not an openStake answer is refused.

## M2.1 23: the invoice path is daemon-blocked, and what it would take

MEASURED BEFORE CLAIMING IT. Across all four packages: no Lightning
dependency of any kind - `blwp-client` has `@noble/curves` and `ws` as dev
deps, `blwp-node` has the same two, `core` and `protocol` have none but

node. Three files mention Lightning at all: two are comments and the third is

declaration of what an operator can do, not an implementation of it.

WHY IT CANNOT BE DONE HERE, from 23.6 rather than from an opinion. The endpoint
that issues, settles and cancels the hold is one of two things:

  - a THRESHOLD-SIGNED LIGHTNING NODE, "FROST-style Schnorr over channel
    operations, VLS-style remote signing generalized: the cleanest fit, and
    EMERGING TECHNOLOGY rather than a solved product"
  - a FEDIMINT-CLASS FEDERATION with a Lightning gateway, "production-ready
    today, with an identical trust statement"

Both are a quorum of separate parties operating real channels. Issuing a hold
invoice, releasing a preimage into it, and cancelling it are operations ON that
quorum - there is no version of them that is arithmetic in this package, which
is what separates them from every 13C piece done so far. 23.1 is explicit: "the
settlement committee's Lightning endpoint (23.6) issues a hold invoice".

23.6 also adds a contract field this repo does not have: "The Round Contract
NAMES WHICH CONSTRUCTION it uses."

THE SHARE OF WHAT 13C STILL OWES, eight pieces:

  issue the hold invoice        daemon: a Lightning endpoint plus 23.6's quorum
  settle it                     daemon, and 5 preimage shares plus 5-of-7
  cancel it                     daemon, and 5-of-7
  let it expire                 DONE - nobody acts, and that is the state
  slashing                      daemon: 5A.3B's bond output, MuSig2, an
                                arbitration quorum
  CLTV sizing                   blocked on a UNIT, not a daemon: the contract
                                measures the round in ticks, an HTLC in time,
                                and no protocol tick rate exists
  the invoice check before
    paying                      NOT BLOCKED. A client must refuse an invoice
                                whose payment hash is not the stakeCommitment
                                its entry contract signed, or whose amount is
                                not stakeMsat. Nothing parses an invoice today,
                                so nothing checks either.
  the 23.6 construction field   NOT BLOCKED. A format decision like
                                objectionWindowMs was.

So four of the eight want a daemon, one wants a unit decision, one is done, and
TWO can be built here. Neither of the two is "issuing, settling or cancelling",
which is what this cut asked for - that is the blocked half, and it is blocked
the same way slashing is.

NOTHING WAS FAKED AND NO ENDPOINT WAS INVENTED. No code changed this turn.

## M2.1 13C: what is still missing, counted, and the one slice that was not blocked

Before opening anything, the gap was counted rather than described. §13C names
four normative things:

  1. the canonical transcript = the longest checkpoint chain five committee
     members receipted, TOGETHER WITH the input batches it commits to, as one
     object every node replays
  2. no quorum + proven equivocation -> FORFEIT
  3. no quorum otherwise -> VOID, refunded by letting the HTLC expire, out of
     the pool and out of the payout table
  4. nodes whose signature contradicts a replay are slashed

Status at ead28a1: 2 and 3 done. 4 daemon-blocked (5A.3B bond output, MuSig2,
an arbitration set). 1 HALF done - the selection was right and the object was
not. So of 4 clauses, 1.5 were missing, and of that 1.5 exactly 0.5 was
buildable here: **one third of what 13C was still missing, and all of the part
that is not waiting on a daemon, a time unit or a discrete-log group.**

The other candidate slice on the list was client backpressure (a reconnect is
tried once, the hold grows without limit while the socket is down). Real, M2.1,
unblocked - and 0 of the 13C gap, so it did not win the turn.

### The collision, measured before it was fixed

Three carried chains over ONE set of three batches:

| node | marks | through tick | last state hash | transcriptHash |
|------|-------|--------------|-----------------|----------------|
| A    | 3     | 12           | 33333333        | f5abe7b64aa9e058 |
| B    | 2     | 9            | 22222222        | f5abe7b64aa9e058 |
| C    | 3     | 12           | **99999999**    | f5abe7b64aa9e058 |

One hash for three objects, therefore one `resultId` (f9cfca55024f7c70) for a
committee to sign - including for node C, whose player had committed to a
different world at the last tick. `PlayerResult` carries `transcriptHash` and
nothing else that names the run, and `objectionHolds` binds an objection to the
same 32 bytes, so both money paths were pinned to the input half only.

The header comment on `transcript.js` had said so plainly since it was written
("Checkpoints belong in it later ... their absence here is why `transcriptHash`
covers the inputs only"). It was a stated hole, not a discovered one; what was
missing was the number that says how much it costs.

### What went in

`transcript.js` gained `marks`: a vector of whole signed checkpoint records,
231 bytes each, no length prefix because nothing in a signed mark is
variable-length. The hash covers the signature, which is the OPPOSITE of the
rule one object down - a checkpoint's own id is taken before it is signed so
the chain does not shift underneath it. The reason is that a transcript is a
container, not an identity: what must be pinned is the bytes a node hands over
and a committee signs a result about, and a signature outside the hash would
let a node serve marks with nobody's signature on them and still match.

`checkTranscript` now returns `{ ok, ticks, marks, throughTick }` and reports
failures as `{ ok: false, in, at, why }`, `in` being 'batch' or 'mark' because
the two are numbered separately. It checks, from the object alone and with no
curve:

  - each mark is for this round and this entry
  - the mark chain links, first to NO_PREVIOUS
  - ticks strictly increase (the same tick twice is 13B, not a chain)
  - every `inputChainHash` is a head this transcript actually reaches - §11's
    "a transcript whose inputs were never published cannot be replayed and
    therefore cannot be finalized as a win", as a refusal
  - the heads do not go backwards (two marks on ONE head is legal: a mark can
    be taken with no input between them; a rewind is not)
  - the last mark commits through the LAST batch, so a node cannot pad the
    canonical object with ticks nobody receipted

`canonicalTranscript` puts the carried prefix's marks in the object it serves.
`handOver` carries none, deliberately: it is the store's own copy for a resume,
where the marks travel on `/checkpoints` and the client checks each against the
receipts it recovered - taking a node's word for its own last mark is exactly
what `resume` refuses to do. The difference between the two objects shows in
the hash instead of being a matter of who is asking.

### Mutants: 11 planted, 11 killed, none retracted

| mutant | protocol red | node red |
|--------|-------------:|---------:|
| unknown input head accepted | 1 | 0 |
| a rewind to earlier inputs allowed | 1 | 0 |
| batches past the last mark allowed | 2 | 0 |
| the same tick twice allowed | 1 | 0 |
| the mark chain unchecked | 1 | 0 |
| another round's mark accepted | 1 | 0 |
| another entry's mark accepted | 1 | 0 |
| a short record accepted | 1 | 0 |
| the marks left out of the encoding | 4 | 2 |
| the node serves no marks | 0 | 6 |
| the node serves every mark it holds | 0 | 2 |

The last two are the ones that matter: a node that served an empty chain or its
whole chain instead of the carried prefix is caught at the node, not only in
the package.

### Suites

protocol 149/149 (was 140), blwp-node 70/70 (was 68), blwp-client 72/72,
core 80/80, money guard 9 files clean, determinism guard 19 files clean.
Unity untouched.

### What 13C still misses after this

Only clause 4, slashing, and it is daemon-blocked. The replay in clause 1 ("all
nodes replay that object") is the committee's, not this repo's: the node
imports no core by law.

## M2.1 backpressure: a VOID run stays VOID when the socket comes back

### The baseline, measured at 8c8c68a before anything was written

The letter's premise was that a reconnect is tried once and the hold grows
without limit. Both halves were already false, and saying so was the first
thing measured.

**Reconnects.** The loop was `blwp.jslib:306-333`: retry forever, backoff
1000 -> 2000 -> 4000 -> 8000ms cap, one attempt in flight on `net.chain`, and
its only stop condition was `net.state === 'gone'`. Its own comment records
that one-attempt was an earlier fault. **0 tests reached it** - all 19
"reconnect" lines in the client suites drive `connect()` + `resume()` by hand,
because the jslib is the one file `node --test` cannot load.

**What grew while down.** Socket closed, 3000 ticks fed at the page's cadence
(a batch every 6th, a mark every 60th), contract `blockTicks: 9000`:

| down-tick | held | marksSkipped | dropped |
|-----------|-----:|-------------:|--------:|
| 600       |   0* |            1 |       0 |
| 1200      |  594 |            1 |       0 |
| 1800      | 1194 |            1 |       0 |
| 2400      | 1794 |            1 |       0 |
| 3000      | 2394 |            1 |       0 |

`said` 0, marks in flight 0, publishes in flight 0. Marks are skipped, never
queued. 550 messages were handed to a socket that was not there, each answered
`error there is no socket`. (*the 0 is `held` under-reporting: up to `chunk` =
600 rows sat inside a doomed publish promise, neither held nor sent.)

**The bound that already existed.** `maxHold = blockTicks` = 9000 ticks = 150s
at 60Hz, and the first tick that will not fit is `dropped=1, ended=true,
ending='VOID'`. Justified in the code, not chosen by taste. Left alone.

### The hole that was actually there

```
ENDED : ended true  ending VOID
ENDED : reason a tick was dropped at 607: the hold was full at 600, so no
        transcript from here can be replayed
ENDED : resume() answered {"ticks":6,"batches":1,"nextTick":6,"receipts":1,
        "live":false,"witnessed":0}
ENDED : after resume, ended true ending VOID nextTick 6 held 600
```

`resume` never looked at `ended`. The jslib then set `net.state = 'ready'` and
logged `resumed at tick 6`. A link the operator owns had ended the player's run
and the page showed a healthy session: status `ready`, the player still
driving, every later tick silently discarded by `record`, nobody told. A
disconnect working as an escape hatch, in the operator's favour.

### What went in

`Client.reconnect(where)` in `packages/blwp-client/src/client.js`: one in
flight whatever the drop rate (a second caller gets the first one's promise),
retries with the same 1s/2s/4s/8s ladder so a two-second node restart does not
end a session, and reads `ended` EVERY time round rather than once on the way
in - the game keeps handing over ticks through an outage, so the run can end
while the loop is asleep. `sleep` is injected, like `sign` and `verify`, so the
ladder can be watched in milliseconds instead of thirty real seconds.

`resume` refuses an ended run by name and returns no numbers. It decides
nothing: `endRun` decided VOID where the fault happened, and this only declines
to re-animate it. No second word is ever set and no outcome is computed in a
browser.

`drain` and `markNow` do not touch the wire with no socket. 550 doomed sends
became 0, and `held` reports 3006 of 3006 instead of reading up to 600 short.

`blwp.jslib` lost its copy of the loop, its `chain`, `tries`, `backoff` and
`drops`, and calls `client.reconnect(net.where)`. When that answers null the
run is over: the page prints the client's own word and reason and goes to
state `ended` - it does not pick one. The status line gained ` ENDED <word>`.

### Mutants: 9 planted, 9 killed, none retracted

| mutant | blwp-client red |
|--------|----------------:|
| reconnect ignores ended (the door) | 2 |
| reconnect ignores ended (the loop) | 2 |
| two reconnects in flight | 1 |
| the backoff never doubles | 1 |
| the backoff has no cap | 1 |
| resume ignores ended | 1 |
| drain sends with no socket | 1 |
| markNow sends with no socket | 1 |
| the hold bound is a taste number (100000) | 4 |

TWO OF THEM KILLED BY STALLING FIRST, and that was fixed rather than counted.
A loop that ignores `ended` goes on opening sockets after its assertion has
already failed, so `node --test` never exited and the runner timed out at 200s
- a suite that stalls says nothing about which rule broke. Both tests now RACE
the loop against a 1000ms wait and assert on the result, and park the loop in
`finally` (`sleep` replaced with a promise that never settles, which holds no
timer so the process can exit). Both then died red, at 2 and 1.

### Suites

blwp-client 79/79 (was 72), blwp-node 70/70, protocol 149/149, core 80/80,
money guard 9 files clean, determinism guard 19 files clean. Unity untouched.

### What this closes

0 of 13C. It was the whole of the remaining unblocked M2.1: PRIORITIES named
exactly one open item there and this was it. What is left of M2.1 is 13C's
slashing, which needs the other six daemons.

## M2.1 backpressure: the session's one word, and the game being told

Two holes an audit found in code no test could load, closed with numbers.

### A - the socket-up VOID, before and after

The page kept `net.state` and learned `ended` from one place only: `reconnect`
answering null, which is the socket-DOWN path. `endRun` closes the socket, and
the close listener's first line is `if (this.ended) return;` - the run is over,
not dropped - so a VOID that happened with the socket still up (a slow node
filling the hold; the case `backpressure.test.js` calls "the first dropped tick
ends the run") reached nothing. Measured on the bridge itself:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `client.state` after a socket-up VOID | (did not exist) | `ended` |
| status line, first word | `ready` | `ended` |
| the same line also carried | `ENDED VOID` | `VOID <reason>` |
| `onEnd` fired | never | once, with word and reason |

Two words about one session, and the first is the one a reader trusts.

The word and the line now live in `client.js`. `opening -> ready -> dropped ->
ready ... -> ended`, terminal, and `status(seen)` builds the panel line where
`node --test` can read its first word. The jslib keeps `net.state` only for the
phase before a client exists: `opening`, or `error` with the client nulled.
`gone` is gone - grep showed three reads and no assignment anywhere, so it had
never been set.

### B - the game was never told

`NetSession.Status` is a string polled twice a second and `git grep` found
nothing consuming it but HUD text. So after a VOID the truck kept driving, the
core kept stepping, and the player finished a round nobody could pay out.

Two exports now: `BlwpNetEnded()` as an int, because it is asked every tick and
on every input read and pinning a 256-byte buffer per frame to be told "no" is
a cost every player pays for the case that has not happened; and
`BlwpNetEnding(ptr, cap)` writing `<WORD> <reason>` or nothing. Both read
`client.ending` and `client.endingReason` and choose neither.

C# consumes them as two rules, static so an editor can read them - `BlwpNet` is
a stub outside a WebGL player, so nothing there will ever answer true:

  CoreDrivenTruck.ShouldStop(driving, ended)      -> stop stepping
  CoreDrivenTruck.LocksControls(locked, ended)    -> take no more input

No combat, no driving, no scoring, no delivery moved into C#. `StopDriving`
hands the rigidbody back the way `OnDisable` already did and logs the reason it
was given. Nothing tells the node: 13C reads what the node already holds, and
no protocol message was invented.

The jslib is one `mergeInto(LibraryManager.library, {...})` call, which is an
object literal. `bridge.test.js` evaluates it with a `mergeInto` that keeps
what it is handed and a fake `Module.HEAPU8`, then drives the three exports
against a REAL client on a REAL node and reads the bytes C# would read. What is
stubbed is Emscripten; nothing that matters is mocked.
