## M2.1 backpressure: the truck stops, and the player is told why

Two holes I named in an audit of my own push, closed with numbers.

### A - the stop handed the truck back to PhysX

`StopDriving` did exactly what `OnDisable` does: `_rb.isKinematic =
_wasKinematic; _truck.externallyDriven = false`. That is the handover TO the
physics controller. `TruckController.controlsLocked` - the real input lock,
`throttle = 0, steerIn = 0, handbrake = true`, the one `LoadoutPanel` and
`SplashScreen` already use - was never set. So the core stopped stepping, the
client published nothing, and the player kept driving a round that could not be
settled. My `Locked` guard only zeroed input INTO the core, which had already
stopped, which is why it looked closed.

One `HandBack(bool lockControls)` now serves both callers, so the three lines
cannot drift again: an ending locks, an ordinary disable does not.

### B - nothing on screen said why

`grep` found no reference to `NetSession`, `BlwpNet` or `Marks` anywhere in
`DriveHud.cs`. The ending went to `Debug.Log` - the browser console. The player
saw a truck stop dead and was told nothing.

`DriveHud.RunStoppedLine(ending)` turns `<WORD> <reason>` into
`RUN STOPPED - <reason>` and DROPS THE WORD. The client's word is `VOID`, and
that is the protocol's name for what a COMMITTEE decides under the no-quorum
rule; a browser announcing it would be the browser-side outcome the whole
design forbids. What this client knows is that it cannot record any more of
this round, so that is what is said. The EditMode test asserts the line
contains none of VOID / REFUND / REFUNDED / WON / LOST / FORFEIT / PAID /
DELIVERED.

### The measurement, and two wrong tests on the way to it

FIRST TRY, `DriveInput.TouchThrottle = 1f` held for two seconds: the truck
moved 0 m. No keyboard is pressed in a batch run and `TouchControls` writes
those fields every frame, so the control measurement failed - which means the
"it did not move once stopped" test beside it, which PASSED, was proving
nothing at all. Switched to `useExternalInput` + `externalThrottle`, which is
what every other PlayMode driving test uses.

SECOND TRY, with a throttle that actually reached the wheels: **the lock test
failed at 3.75 m**. That was the honest answer to a badly framed question - a
loaded truck at speed coasts, and the window started half a second after the
lock. Coasting to a halt is not driving. So the test now gives it the three
seconds a loaded truck needs, asserts it is AT REST (< 0.5 m/s), and only then
watches for two seconds with the throttle still down.

Final, all three green:

| | measured |
|---|---|
| alive, throttle 1.0, 2s | moved > 1 m (the control) |
| stopped, throttle still 1.0 | at rest, < 0.5 m over 2 s |
| `controlsLocked` after the stop | true |
| `externallyDriven` after the stop | false |
| ordinary handover (`OnDisable`) | `controlsLocked` false - still the player's truck |

| mutant | platform | red |
|--------|----------|----:|
| the stop does not lock the truck | PlayMode | 1 of 3 |
| an ordinary handover locks it too | PlayMode | 1 of 3 |
| the HUD prints the protocol word | EditMode | 3 of 189 (2 new) |
| the HUD says nothing at all | EditMode | 3 of 189 (2 new) |

## M2.1 backpressure: the door, photographed on the built player

PlayMode shows the truck at rest under real physics and EditMode shows the
wording. Neither is a browser, and the jslib and the C# only take effect in a
WebGL build - so the door was driven on the built page: a real blwp-node, the
real player over HTTP, a real Chrome, the node taken away entirely.

The harness is kept as `packages/blwp-client/tools/screen.mjs`. It builds a
bond into a block mined on top of Bitcoin's REAL genesis header, because
`discover` anchors on genesis and refuses one the page supplies; serves the
headers from two ports so the two-source floor is met by two origins rather
than two calls; and injects the round, entry and providers into the built
`index.html` after the client bundle.

### Three refusals on the way in, each the door working

  - `bond provider 0 does not say which source it is` - a bond provider needs
    a declared tag, exactly as a header provider does.
  - `the advertisement for 2694e2e6... is not signed by the node it names` -
    an advertisement signed by a stranger is not the committee's.
  - and then it opened: **rounds 1, entries 1, batches 33, checkpoints 1**,
    asked of the node's own store rather than inferred from a quiet console.

### FAULT 1, and only a browser could have found it

    [blwp] run ended VOID: a tick was dropped at NaN: the hold was full at 0

Every session VOIDed on its first tick, before a byte was published.
`Client.at` resolves three round trips before `setRound` does - open, join,
connect - and Unity ticks at 60 Hz through all of them, so `record` ran against
a client whose `maxHold` was still the constructor's 0 and whose `offered` was
`undefined++`, which is NaN. Every test in the client suite calls `setRound`
before it records anything; the game does not.

It predates this door and it was INVISIBLE, because nothing was told: the page
went on looking healthy while the client had quietly given up. It shows now
only because a VOID stops the truck. `record` refuses when there is no round -
the entry's `joinTick` is what says where a transcript begins - and the mutant
that removes the guard is 1 red.

### FAULT 2, photographed

The RUN STOPPED banner was hung off `UnderFireBox` and landed straight across
"BLOCK 965,982 · 0:55" and the drop-off marker: two lines of yellow over each
other. The horizontal rule this file records learning four times - the gap
between the columns, never the whole width - had been obeyed, and the vertical
one had never been asked. It is a row of the same headline stack the price, the
liquidation line and the block clock are rows of now, starting where the block
clock's box ends, and an EditMode test asserts that at 1280x660, 1920x1080,
844x390 and 390x844.

### The measurement, on the built page

The headless renderer draws about eleven frames a second, not sixty - measured,
90 held ticks in the first eight - so a 1800-tick round takes some 165 seconds
of outage to fill rather than thirty. Watched rather than assumed:

    +8s    dropped held  102  ... tries 2
    +40s   dropped held  478  ... tries 6
    +88s   dropped held  982  ... tries 10
    +136s  dropped held 1446  ... tries 14
    +176s  ended   held 1800 offered 2187 maxHold 1800 tries 17 ENDED VOID

    [blwp] run ended VOID: a tick was dropped at 2187: the hold was full at
           1800, so no transcript from here can be replayed
    [blwp] the core stopped driving: VOID a tick was dropped at 2187 ...

Seventeen reconnect attempts over 176 seconds, one loop, never abandoned; the

| on the built page | before the stop | after it |

None of VOID / REFUND / WON / LOST / FORFEIT / PAID / DELIVERED is on that

## M2.1 5A.3B: the slash law, and the line between law and enforcement

### The gap, counted before anything was written

`grep -rn slash packages/*/src` returned **0**. §5A.3 names six offences and
§5A.3B gives five steps from proof to transaction; the repo held none of it.

The five steps, and which of them actually need somebody:

  1. anyone publishes a fraud proof                      - PURE
  2. the proof is mechanically checked - "either a signature comparison or a
     deterministic replay. No judgement."                - PURE
  3. k-of-m arbitration keys sign a spend of path B      - DAEMON
  4. the transaction carries OP_RETURN = H(fraud_proof)  - PURE
  5. outputs pay the distribution the contract fixes     - DAEMON

So PRIORITIES' old line - "slashing needs the other six daemons" - was too
broad. The LAW is pure and the ENFORCEMENT is not, and only the second half was
ever blocked.

### The slice, and its share

§13C names exactly one slashing case, its clause 3: "nodes whose signature
contradicts a replay of the canonical transcript are slashed", which is row 2
of §5A.3's table. §13C has four clauses and three were in, so **this is the
last 1 of the 4 things 13C names**, and 1 of the 6 offences in 5A.3.

The replay verdict is INJECTED, exactly as §13A's `objectionHolds` injects it.
This package steps no simulation and the daemon imports no core.

### What went in

`packages/protocol/src/slash.js`: `SlashProof` (type 0x0c, tag
`BLWP/v1/SlashProof`, both the next free number rather than a reuse) carrying
round, player, node, the canonical transcript hash, the accused result's id,
and the bond outpoint; `slashProofId`; `slashCommitment`, which is what step 4
requires the OP_RETURN to carry; and `slashHolds`.

Eight checks, every one a comparison:

  - the accused is on this round's committee - a stranger's signature is not
    misconduct, and `provisionallyFinal` already ignores it
  - the attached evidence IS the result the proof names, by id
  - that result was signed by the accused, for this round, for this player
  - the proof names the canonical transcript, AND so did the result - a node
    that signed about another object answered a different question, which is
    13C's no-quorum case and not a slashing one
  - the bond is the outpoint the node's OWN advertisement committed to, txid
    and vout both - an accuser who could name the outpoint would be naming
    anybody's money
  - and the one judgement, handed in: anything but an explicit `true` leaves
    the bond alone, because 5A.3B's own residual is that an attesting party
    "can, in principle, slash without cause"

Deliberately not here: the distribution ("half to the affected players, half
burned or to the remaining honest committee members, as fixed by the Round
Contract") needs a contract field that does not exist, and adding one moves
every round id. The retrieval hint of step 4 is not here either - the spec
does not fix its shape, and inventing one would be inventing a second
protocol. `OFFENCES` holds one name, not six: a name that answers nothing
reads as coverage.

### The before/after, which is the test this slice exists for

Same proof, same evidence, same bond; only the replay verdict moves.

| | `replayDiffers: false` | `replayDiffers: true` |
|---|---|---|
| `slashed` | false | true |
| `bond` | **undefined - not even named** | `{txid 5555…, vout 3}` |
| `offence` | - | `REPLAY_CONTRADICTS` |
| `commitment` | - | `slashProofId(proof)`, what the OP_RETURN carries |
| why | no replay has contradicted the signed result | the node signed a result the canonical transcript does not replay to |

### Mutants: 14 planted, 14 killed, none retracted

| mutant | protocol red |
|--------|-------------:|
| a claim is enough to slash | 2 |
| a truthy verdict is enough (`!replayDiffers`) | 1 |
| the accuser names the bond | 1 |
| the vout is not part of the bond | 1 |
| any advertisement will do | 1 |
| the evidence need not be the accused result | 1 |
| somebody else's signature counts | 1 |
| another round counts | 1 |
| another player counts | 1 |
| the proof may name any transcript | 1 |
| a result about another transcript counts | 1 |
| a stranger can be slashed | 1 |
| the bond vout left out of the commitment | 2 |
| the transcript left out of the commitment | 2 |

The last two matter most: a commitment that does not cover the whole proof is
a slash a stranger cannot re-verify, and 5A.3B's whole audit story rests on
being able to.

## M2.1 5A.3 row 3: a payout table that is not F of its published inputs

**This accounts for 1 of the 5 that was missing** - five §5A.3 rows were
unenforced after `REPLAY_CONTRADICTS`, and four are now.

### Why this row and not another

§20 is what makes it mechanical: "PayoutTable = F(RoundContract, Membership,
FinalResults). Deterministic. Nodes sign the payout-table hash... A node
signing a table that does not equal F(...) of its published inputs is
slashable." `F` is `computePayoutTable` and it already lives in this package,
so unlike the replay row **nothing is injected**: no attesting party is needed
and 5A.3B's residual - an attester who "can, in principle, slash without
cause" - does not reach this row at all.

### The one decision, made in the open

§20 fixes `F` and says the table's HASH is signed; it does not fix the bytes
that hash is taken over. `TYPE_PAYOUT_TABLE = 0x07` and the tag
`BLWP/v1/PayoutTable` were reserved before anything used them, so the encoding
fills a reserved slot the way the objection did when the spec gave a field list
and no layout. Two things went into it deliberately:

  - THE ROUND ID. Without it a table is a list of amounts that could belong to
    any round with the same players, and a signature would carry across rounds.
    Mutant "the round is left out of the table": **11 red**, the loudest of the
    battery, because half the vectors hang off that id.
  - SORTED BY PUBKEY. `computePayoutTable` returns rows in the caller's entry
    order, so two honest nodes handed the same entries in a different order
    would otherwise sign different bytes and `F` being deterministic would buy
    nothing.

### The inputs are the node's, not the accuser's

Row 3 is about a table against "its published inputs", so a proof that did not
name them would be an accusation with a free variable: whoever checks it later
recomputes from a different membership and gets a different answer.
`payoutInputsId` commits to the membership - pubkey, outcome, score, stake -
and the score floor, sorted the way `F` sorts, so two people publishing the
same inputs commit to the same 32 bytes. It rides in the proof's existing
`transcriptHash` field, which means "the object this offence is measured
against": a transcript for the replay row, the inputs for this one. One field,
one meaning, and no widening of a body that is already committed to on chain.

### The before and after

Same node, same bond, same published inputs; one millisatoshi moved.

| | honest table | one msat short |
|---|---|---|
| `slashed` | false | true |
| `bond` | **undefined - not even named** | `{txid 5555…, vout 3}` |
| `offence` | - | `TABLE_IS_NOT_F` |
| `expected` | - | the id of F's own table, so the accusation is checkable |
| why | the table signed is exactly F of its published inputs | the table signed is not F of the inputs the node published |

A millisatoshi moved BETWEEN two players - a table that still sums correctly -
is also not F, and is also slashed.

### A rough edge the tests found

`slashHoldsOnTable` threw `u64 needs a BigInt` out of the input commitment when
handed entries with a number stake, which hands a caller that asked for a
verdict an exception instead. The caller least able to cope with that is a node
acting on somebody else's accusation, so malformed inputs are now refused by
name like every other check here.

## M2.1 5A.3 row 4: a settlement action 23.2 did not authorise

**This accounts for 1 of the 4 that were missing**, and three remain.

### Why this row of the four

By count the four are equal, so the pick was by the class named: a
deterministic recomputation with no attester injected. Row 4 is the only one of
the four whose `F` is already in this package - `settlementAction` IS §23.2's
table, and `SETTLEMENT_THRESHOLD` is its 5. Row 1 (two results for one player)
is a signature comparison rather than a recomputation; rows 5 and 6 need rules
the repo does not hold - §5A.13's `operator_id` linkage and §22A's availability.

It is also the only one of the four where the player's money has ALREADY LEFT
THEM when the offence happens: §23.2's SETTLE is the single direction that
takes a stake.

### What went in

`TYPE_SETTLEMENT_RECORD = 0x0d` and `BLWP/v1/SettlementRecord`, both the next
free number, because the spec names the record as a proof and gives it no
encoding. The record is what a node DID and the conditions it published for
having done it: round, entry, node, action, outcome, qualification, state,
shares, signatures. The entry is in it because a settlement action is about one
player's hold invoice - without it the action is against no particular money
and its signature would carry to any entry of the round.

`ACTIONS` / `actionByte` / `actionOf` in payout.js, so the three words have a
wire byte and two implementations cannot spell one action two ways.
`outcomeOf` in result.js, the inverse `decodePlayerResult` had inline - two
copies of one mapping is two places for a byte to come to mean different
things. ENTRY_VOID deliberately has no byte: widening `OUTCOMES` would move
every result id, and §23.2 gives VOID and ENTRY_VOID the same action anyway.

### Two ways to be wrong, and one that is not

  - the counts the node itself published do not meet §23.2's requirements
  - the action is not the one those conditions call for - settling where 23.2
    cancels takes a qualifier's own stake into the pool WITH the signatures
    that authorise a cancel, so the counts are met and the money still went
    the wrong way

And DOING LESS IS NOT AN OFFENCE. §23.2: "the default path - nobody acting - is
always the refund. That is what makes infrastructure failure safe." A node that
acted on nothing has taken nothing from anybody, and slashing for it would
invert the one direction the design is built to keep safe: an operator could be
punished for leaving a player their money.

### The before and after

One loser's stake, one settlement, and the only thing that moves is a count the
node published about itself.

| | 5 signatures | 4 signatures |
|---|---|---|
| `slashed` | false | true |
| `bond` | **undefined - not even named** | `{txid 5555…, vout 3}` |
| `offence` | - | `SETTLED_WITHOUT_AUTHORITY` |
| why | 23.2 authorised SETTLE on those conditions | SETTLE needed 4 of 5 settlement signatures |

Every one of §23.2's five conditions on a settle was measured separately -
signatures, shares, a result that is PROVISIONALLY_FINAL, one that is
SUSPENDED, and one that is not final at all - and each is slashed. A qualifier
settled with a FULL seven signatures is slashed too, `due: CANCEL`.

### A test of mine that was measuring nothing

"a stranger cannot be slashed" left the PROOF naming a committee member while
only the record named the stranger, so it stopped at "written by a different
node" and never reached the committee check it claimed to be about. It passed
either way, which is the worst kind. Fixed, not loosened.

`OFFENCES` was asserted in whichever file added a row last, so every new row
broke the previous file's count. It is a claim about the MODULE, so it now
lives once in `slash.test.js` and adding row 5 touches that line and no other.

## M2.1 5A.3 row 4: the two fields the row had left free

Found auditing my own row before answering whether it was finished, and fixed
on the row rather than parked.

`SlashProof` has one body across all rows. Rows 2 and 3 pin every field of it:
row 2 checks `transcriptHash` against the canonical transcript and
`playerPubkey` against the signed result, row 3 checks `transcriptHash` against
the published inputs. **Row 4 checked neither.** Measured by reading the file:
`playerPubkey` and `transcriptHash` appear at lines 181, 191, 193 and 292 -
rows 2 and 3 - and nowhere in `slashHoldsOnSettlement`.

Two free variables in a body whose hash goes on chain. What that costs:

  - an accuser can vary them at will and mint unboundedly many DIFFERENT valid
    proofs of one offence, each with a different commitment, which is exactly
    what 5A.3B's "every slash is permanently auditable" rests on not happening
  - and the record names an ENTRY, not a player, so a free `playerPubkey` puts
    somebody's name on a settlement that was never about them - a reader of the
    proof takes them for the victim

Pinned: `transcriptHash` must be the record's own `entryId` - "the object this
offence is measured against" is the entry whose hold invoice was acted on - and
`playerPubkey` must be thirty-two zero bytes, because this row names no player
directly. Required to be EMPTY rather than plausible: a field this row does not
use should be checkably unused, not merely unchecked.

Mutants: "the proof may name any entry" 1 red, "the proof may name any player"
1 red. 17 planted on this row in total now, 17 killed, none retracted.

unchanged and not re-run for theatre - no file outside `packages/protocol`
moved. Unity untouched.

## M2.1 5A.3 row 1: a node that signs two different results for one player

The first row of the table in document order, and the last of the four whose
`F` or comparison this package already had. **Four of 5A.3's six rows are now
written; two remain** - row 5 (signing for a round the operator played, 5A.13)
and row 6 (a fee share without the availability rule, 22A).

### The purest of the four

Rows 3 and 4 recompute an `F`; row 2 needs somebody to have replayed. This one
only COMPARES, so no attesting party enters at any point and 5A.3B's residual -
an attester who "can, in principle, slash without cause" - does not touch it.
The two objects ARE the offence, which is what 5A.3 means by "a portable
artifact anyone can check".

It is 13B's rule with the sides swapped. There, two marks at one tick forfeit a
PLAYER's stake; here, two results about one player cost a NODE its bond. Both
are a signature comparison and neither needs a curve in this package: whose
signature it is stays the caller's, the same boundary `provesEquivocation`
draws.

### One offence, one commitment

5A.3 row 1 is about a PAIR, and a pair that could be written either way round
is two proofs of one offence with two different hashes. 5A.3B step 4 puts
H(fraud_proof) on chain and rests "every slash is permanently auditable" on it,
so an offence that could be minted twice is one an auditor cannot tell from two
separate offences.

`orderedResultIds` sorts the two ids by their bytes: the LOWER is the one the
proof names in `signedResultId`, the higher rides in `transcriptHash`, which on
every row means "the object this offence is measured against" - a transcript on
row 2, the published inputs on row 3, the entry on row 4, the other result
here. Measured: handing the evidence in either order gives the same commitment,
and a proof that names them the other way round is REFUSED rather than being a
second valid proof of the same thing.

### The before and after

| | the same result twice | two different results |
|---|---|---|
| `slashed` | false | true |
| `bond` | **undefined - not even named** | `{txid 5555…, vout 3}` |
| `offence` | - | `TWO_RESULTS` |
| why | those are the same result, signed twice | the node signed two different results for one player of one round |

A repeat is not a contradiction, exactly as it is not one in 13B: taking a bond
for a retransmission would punish a dropped socket. Re-signing one result with
a different 64 bytes is still one result - the id is taken over the body, and
the signature sits beside it.

Two nodes disagreeing is NOT this offence - that is 13C's no-quorum case, which
voids or forfeits an entry and must take nobody's bond - and two results about
different players or different rounds are two honest answers.

| mutant | protocol red |
|--------|-------------:|
| a repeat is an offence | 2 |
| the pair may be named either way | 2 |
| only the named id is pinned | 1 (was **0**, see below) |
| only the other id is pinned | 1 |
| the order is the call order | 2 |
| any number of results is a pair | 1 |
| another node signing counts | 1 |
| another round counts | 1 |
| another player counts | 1 |
| a stranger can be double-signed against | 1 |
| the bond is the accuser's to name | 1 |
| any advertisement will do | 1 |

**ONE SURVIVED AT 0 RED and it was the same hole row 4 had.** Checking only
`signedResultId` and dropping the `transcriptHash` half left every test green,
because the swap test moves BOTH fields at once and the single-field check
still catches that. So `transcriptHash` was not actually pinned by anything - a
free variable in a body whose hash goes on chain, for the second row running. A
test now asserts each half of the pair alone, and the mutant dies at 1.

That is twice in two rows. The shared `SlashProof` body is the reason: a field
that means something different on each row is a field each row has to be shown
to pin, and a test that moves two of them together shows neither.

## M2.1 5A.3 row 5: signing for a round the declared operator played

The next unwritten row in document order. **Five of 5A.3's six rows are
written; one remains** - row 6, a fee share claimed without §22A's availability
rule. Rows 5 and 6 are ordinary offences, not enforcement: the enforcement that
stays parked is 5A.3B steps 3 and 5, the k-of-m arbitration signature and the
broadcast.

### The law

5A.13: "A selected node may not sign anything for a round in which its operator
has an Entry Contract... If a selected node's `operator_id` also signed an Entry
Contract in that round, the node is conflicted: its result signatures,
payout-table signatures and settlement participation are invalid, and it earns
no fee share. Signing anyway is a slashable offence with a one-artifact proof."

Nothing is injected. Like rows 1, 3 and 4 this only reads what two objects
already say.

### BEING CONFLICTED IS NOT THE OFFENCE. SIGNING IS.

An operator may play a round their node was selected for. What 5A.13 forbids is
that node SIGNING in it, and its own remedy for a committee pushed under
threshold by conflicts is ENTRY_VOID - a refund - not somebody's bond. A
conflicted node that signed nothing has taken nothing from anybody, and the
check returns no slash for it. That is this row's doing-nothing path and it has
its own test and its own mutant ("being conflicted is the offence", 1 red).

### The one decision, made in the open

5A.13 calls `operator_id` "a pubkey" AND "a self-declaration... not a proof of
identity". This package already carried it as a STRING for the second reason -
`advert.js` says so at the line that encodes it - so reading one as a key is
done in `operatorKeyOf` and nowhere else: sixty-four LOWERCASE hex characters,
the way `toHex` writes a key, and anything else declares nobody.

That is not a weakness of the check, it is 5A.13's own scope, in its words: "an
attacker who runs nodes and plays simply declares nothing, or declares
unrelated ids, and the rule does not fire... defence in depth, not a Sybil
control." Measured: an empty string, a word, 63 hex characters, 66, and the
same key in UPPERCASE all declare nobody and conflict with nobody.

### All three signatures, by the byte the object already carries

5A.13 names result signatures, payout-table signatures and settlement
participation. All three are encodable here now, and each object's first byte
says which it is - so no discriminator was invented and no caller declares one.
A payout table carries no signer of its own (the signature sits beside it), so
the node it accuses is the proof's; a result and a settlement record carry one
and it must be the accused's.

### The before and after

| | the entry is a stranger's | the entry is the declared operator's |
|---|---|---|
| `slashed` | false | true |
| `bond` | **undefined - not even named** | `{txid 5555…, vout 3}` |
| `offence` | - | `OPERATOR_PLAYED` |
| `signed` | - | `result` / `payout table` / `settlement record` |
| why | 5A.13 fires on a DECLARED conflict and nothing else | the node's declared operator has an entry in this round, and it signed a … anyway |

### Mutants: 15 planted, 15 killed, none retracted

| mutant | protocol red |
|--------|-------------:|
| any entry conflicts with any operator | 1 |
| an undeclared operator conflicts too | 1 |
| any string is read as a key | 1 |
| a short declaration is padded into a key | 1 |
| being conflicted is the offence | 1 |
| the proof may name any player | 1 |
| the proof may be measured against any entry | 1 |
| the object need not be the named one | 1 |
| another round's entry counts | 1 |
| another round's object counts | 1 |
| another node signing counts | 1 |
| a stranger can be slashed for a conflict | 1 |
| any advertisement will do | 1 |
| the bond is the accuser's to name | 1 |
| only results count, not tables or records | 1 |

THE PAIR WAS PINNED ONE HALF AT A TIME FROM THE START. Rows 4 and 1 each lost a
mutant to the opposite mistake - a test moving two proof fields together shows
neither pinned - so `playerPubkey` and `transcriptHash` have a test each here,
and the two mutants that move only one of them die at 1 apiece.

## M2.1 5A.3 row 6: claiming a fee share 22A did not earn

The last unwritten row. **All six of 5A.3's rows now have a predicate.** What
remains of slashing is 5A.3B steps 3 and 5 - the k-of-m arbitration signature
and the broadcast - which is a daemon and stays parked.

### The law

22A: "A selected node earns its share only if it performed the contract-defined
minimum service: for game/verify, the required receipts plus replay and
signing; for settlement, participation in the settlement protocol during the
settlement window. A conflicted node (5A.13) never qualifies. Unearned shares
are redistributed pro rata among the other eligible nodes in the same role
pool, keeping the total at 2%."

Two ways to fail it, both in that one paragraph: the service was not performed,
or the node was CONFLICTED and so never qualifies however much it served. The
second reuses row 5's `operatorKeyOf` rather than a second copy of 5A.13.

### CLAIMING NOTHING IS NOT AN OFFENCE

22A's own remedy for a share nobody earned is REDISTRIBUTION - "keeping the
total at 2%" - not a bond. A node that served nothing and claimed nothing has
cost nobody anything, and the check returns no slash for it. That is this row's
doing-nothing path, with its own test and its own mutant (1 red).

### The measurement that shaped it: there is no minimum in the contract

22A says "the contract-defined minimum service". Measured against
`encodeRoundContract`: it carries simCoreHash, the two times, the objection
window, custody, census height and root, committee seed, stake, bond floor,
block ticks, the five exposure numbers, minScore, the rank curve and the nodes.
**There is no minimum-service field.**

So the number is handed in and BOUND into the proof by `feeInputsId`, the same
discipline row 3 needed for its inputs: an accusation whose threshold the
accuser picks after the fact makes every honest claim slashable by choosing a
higher number. The precedent is `minScore`, which `computePayoutTable` also
takes as an argument - the difference is that minScore HAS a contract field to
be read from and this does not.

Naming the field is what would make one minimum canonical for a network, and a
new contract field moves every round id and every vector - the same blocker the
slash distribution has. Listed, not invented.

### Two new objects, one job each

`TYPE_FEE_CLAIM = 0x0e` and `TYPE_SERVICE_RECORD = 0x0f`, next free numbers.
The claim carries round, node, ROLE and amount - 22A pays the two pools
separately and "an operator selected for both roles earns both shares", so a
claim that did not say which role would be a claim on either. The record
carries the same three plus `served`, one count in the unit its own role is
measured in: receipts for game and verify, settlement participations for
settlement. One count and not two schemes - the roles are measured in different
units and the rule over them is the same rule.

### The before and after

| | served 20 of 20 | served 19 of 20 |
|---|---|---|
| `slashed` | false | true |
| `bond` | **undefined - not even named** | `{txid 5555…, vout 3}` |
| `offence` | - | `FEE_WITHOUT_SERVICE` |
| `served` / `required` | - | 19 / 20 |
| `conflicted` | - | false |
| why | it served 20 of the 20 its role required, and 22A is what that fee is for | it claimed a verify share having served 19 of 20 |

And a conflicted node that served 120 of 20 is slashed anyway, `conflicted:
true` - 22A's own sentence.

| mutant | protocol red |
|--------|-------------:|

| serving exactly the minimum is not enough | 3 |
| a conflicted node still qualifies | 1 |

| the minimum is the accuser's to pick | 2 |
| the claim need not be the named one | 1 |
| a claim in another role counts | 1 |
| another round's claim counts | 1 |
| another node's claim counts | 1 |
| another round's record counts | 1 |
| another node's record counts | 1 |
| any minimum is a minimum | 1 |
| a conflict in another round counts | 1 |
| an undeclared operator is a conflict | 1 |

| the role is left out of the binding | 1 |
| the record is left out of the binding | 2 |

The proof's two pinned fields - the claim id and the bound record-and-minimum -
have a test each and a mutant each that moves only one of them. That was the
fault rows 1 and 4 each lost a mutant to, and it has not recurred since row 5.

### One test of mine, corrected

`JSON.stringify` cannot serialise a BigInt and one of the claim's fields is
millisatoshi, so a message helper threw. Named by field rather than by value.
The assertion itself was not touched.

## M2.1: the two slash numbers become signed contract fields

A SIGNED-OBJECT FORMAT CHANGE, made once, the way `objectionWindowMs` was.
Until this the slash law took its threshold and its payout split as arguments,
and a number the caller picks is a number the operator picks - the same fault
the objection window was moved into the contract to fix, and worse here,
because these decide whether a bond is taken and who gets it.

### Measured first, before touching a signed object

  construction sites   20, by grep for the field that went in last time
  vectors that move    ONE. `contracts.json` is the only vector that builds a
                       contract; `checkpoint.json` and `payout.json` carry a
                       round id as opaque bytes and did not move. Predicted
                       from the objectionWindowMs entry above, then confirmed
                       by regenerating: 1 file changed, 4 insertions.
  round id derived in  one place. `roundId(contract)` in contracts.js, called
                       from blwp-node/round.js:198, blwp-client/client.js:174
                       and :279, and the jslib at 276 and 278. No second
                       derivation anywhere.
  the contract grew    270 -> 275 bytes
  the sample round id  99307d45fc3305f5... -> b1cb45543f2d708d...

### The two fields, and the one that is deliberately NOT a field

`slashMinimumServed` (u32). 22A: "A selected node earns its share only if it
performed the CONTRACT-DEFINED minimum service". Now read off the contract by
`slashHoldsOnFeeClaim`, which refuses outright when the contract names none.

`slashRemainder` (u8, BURN or COMMITTEE). 5A.3: "half to the affected players
of that round, half burned or to the remaining honest committee members of the
round, AS FIXED BY THE ROUND CONTRACT." The alternative in that sentence is
what a round fixes.

THE HALVES ARE A CONSTANT, `SLASH_TO_PLAYERS_BPS = 5000`, and that is a
decision made in the open. The spec states them as numbers rather than as a
range, and a contract field for the proportion would let an operator write
itself the whole bond - which is the fault a contract field exists to prevent,
not one to import. Two mutants pin it: setting it to 10000 or to 0 is 3 red
each.

### The distribution, pure and moving nothing

`slashDistribution` says who is owed what out of a bond that has been spent;
spending it is 5A.3B steps 3 and 5 and is not here. The accused is not among
"the REMAINING honest committee members" - a node collects no share of its own
slashing. Remainders are handed out one satoshi at a time in ascending
`H(roundId || pubkey)`, the order 22A names for fees and `payout.js` already
uses for the pool, and with nobody to pay that half is BURNED, which is the
only direction that cannot quietly become somebody's income.

|--------|-------------:|
| the minimum is not in the round id | 2 |
| the destination is not in the round id | 1 |
| a contract without a minimum is accepted | 1 |
| the caller may still pass a minimum | 5 |
| the minimum is left out of the binding | 2 |
| the players' half is a whole bond | 3 |
| the players' half is nothing | 3 |
| a burn pays the committee anyway | 1 |
| nobody to pay means somebody keeps it | 1 |

ONE SURVIVED AT 0 RED and it was a real gap: dropping the round from the
remainder order left every test green, because the test only checked that the
total still added up - which it does whoever gets the satoshi. Measured to fix

Asserted concretely, and the mutant then dies at 1.

RETRACTED, not counted: "the distribution need not add up" removes the

above it is right, so no test kills it without introducing a second fault. It
is a defence against a future change - the same shape as `computePayoutTable`'s
own paid-against-staked throw - and it stays, uncounted.

## M2.1: two money-law holes on the slash-table work, found by auditing my own push

Both were green and wrong, which is the worst kind. Neither was found by a
test; both were found by asking what a caller could still choose.

### HOLE A - the score floor was still the prover's

`slashHoldsOnTable({ ..., entries, minScore = 0 })` took the floor as an
argument, defaulted to zero, while `minScore` has been a signed field of the
round contract all along. Binding it into `payoutInputsId` stopped an accuser
SWAPPING it after the fact and did nothing about them CHOOSING it: whoever
writes the proof picks the floor.

Measured on one set of entries: F is `f5abb801d78b2153` at a floor of 0 and
`f69f32a60d912403` at 999. Two different honest tables, so a prover naming 999
slashes a node whose table was right.

Fixed the same way the fee minimum was: read `contract.minScore`, and refuse
outright when no contract is given. Mutant "the floor is a caller argument
again" is **7 red**.

### HOLE B - the accused could be paid out of its own bond

`slashDistribution` said "the accused is not one of the remaining honest
committee members" in a comment and took `honestCommittee` as given. Measured
before the filter: listing the slashed node returned **25000 of 100000
satoshi** of its own bond. A documented claim that is not a check is not a
check, and this one let an operator write itself the bond through a door the
halves constant does not cover.

AND THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG, which the numbers caught. Filtering the excluded
member out and dividing among the rest took the surviving member from 25000 to
50000 - paying the survivors MORE the more of their colleagues were caught,
which is a reward for a round going wrong. The divisor is the whole set now and
the excluded shares BURN: accused 0, survivor 25000 unchanged, burned 25000.
Every node slashed in the round is out, not only the accused, or two caught
together would each collect from the other's bond.

| mutant | protocol red |
|--------|-------------:|
| the floor is a caller argument again | 7 |
| a contract without a floor is accepted | 1 |
| the floor is read as zero | 3 |
| the slashed node is paid its own bond | 2 |
| only the accused is excluded, not the others | 1 |
| the excluded share is spread over the rest | 2 |
| the excluded share is quietly dropped | 2 |
| an excluded member still takes a leftover satoshi | 1 (was **0**) |

THE LAST ONE SURVIVED AT 0 RED and the reason was in my test, not the code: I

## M2.1 22A: the fee table, and claiming more than it owes

The fee was the one number in this protocol nobody recomputed. Measured before
writing anything: `grep` for gross volume, a fee rate, a pool share or a per-
slot share across `packages/*/src` returned **nothing**, and `feeMsat` - which
every Entry Contract signs and every player pays - was written at
`contracts.js:128`, decoded at 145, and **read by no code at all**. 5A.3 row 6
decided WHETHER a node qualifies; nothing said what the share IS, so a
qualifying node could claim any amount and no predicate contradicted it.

### What went in

`packages/protocol/src/fee.js`, integer BigInt millisatoshi throughout and on
the money guard, which is now 11 files.

  gross      the sum of stakes of financially ACTIVATED entries. Not a second
             predicate: `isRefund` is the same one `computePayoutTable` uses
             for `activated`, because a refunded entry is money that never
             moved and charging a fee on it would charge for a round the player
             was refunded out of.
  the fee    2% of gross, then 1% to each pool - and THE SECOND POOL IS THE
             REMAINDER OF THE FEE, not a second division. Two floors of the
             same ragged number lose a millisatoshi between them; measured
             across 1, 3, 7, 99, 100001, 123457 and 999999999 msat stakes, the
             pools sum to exactly the fee every time.
  who earns  the eligible seats of that pool, and an unearned share is
             redistributed INSIDE the pool - 22A's "keeping the total at 2%".
             Measured: one eligible seat of seven takes the whole 4000 and the
             fee does not grow.
  remainders floored, then handed out one millisatoshi at a time in
             `remainderOrder` - the rule already in `payout.js`, exported
             rather than copied, so there is one implementation of it.
  nobody     a pool no one qualified for is `unallocated`, NOT income. 22A
             keeps the total at 2% by redistributing inside a role pool, and
             with nobody eligible there is no inside. The spec hands it
             nowhere, and nowhere is the only direction that cannot become the
             operator's.

### A fault the first version had, found by a test that failed honestly

The table was keyed by pubkey alone, so a node sitting in both pools had its
two shares MERGED - and a settlement claim was then measured against the
game/verify share and passed. 22A is explicit the other way: "An operator
selected for both roles earns both shares, because it performs both services."
Seats are keyed by pool and key now, `feeOwed` takes the role, and `relay` -
which 22A pays from neither committee - is owed nothing. The mutant that merges
them is **16 red**, the loudest of the battery.

### The over-claim

`slashHoldsOnFeeClaim` recomputes the claim against the table. Claiming more
than owed is the same offence as claiming without service - both take fee money
the round did not earn for that node - and the table is BOUND into the proof by
`feeInputsId`, because a number an accuser recomputes from an eligibility set
of their choosing makes every honest claim an over-claim.

  claimed 4000, owed 4000    not slashed
  claimed 4001, owed 4000    SLASHED, over-claim
  claimed 1, owed 4000       not slashed - asking for less is not an offence
  claimed 0                  not slashed, as before
  claimed for `relay`        SLASHED: owed 0, because no pool pays that role

| the table is left out of the binding | 1 |
| the table need not add up | **RETRACTED** |

RETRACTED for the same reason as the slash distribution's: `paid + unallocated
!== fee` cannot fire while the arithmetic above it is right, so no test kills it
without introducing a second fault. It stays, uncounted.

### THE REPORT ASKED FOR: what checking entry `feeMsat` would need

It needs a decision first, because **the spec contradicts itself**, and the
contradiction is arithmetic rather than editorial:

  18                "Node fees and the player-selected donation are charged ON
                    TOP of the stake at entry and therefore do not reduce the
                    pool."
  22A, Collection   "*(changed)*... wallet commitment 100 sat; node fee 2 sat;
                    donation 2 sat; net game stake 96 sat -> the pool. Earlier
                    versions collected the fee and the donation on top."

They give different fee bases, and 22A's own worked example follows 18 rather
than its own Collection section:

  22A's example        61 x 100 sat = 6,100 sat gross, so 2% = 122 sat
  if stake is NET      61 x 96 = 5,856 sat, so 2% = 117.12 sat - and not an
                       integer number of satoshi
  what 61 players pay  2 sat each = 122 sat

So the base that makes 22A's own numbers work is the WALLET COMMITMENT, while
its Collection section calls the pool contribution the stake. This repo follows
18: `computePayoutTable` says fees are charged on top and never appear in the
table, and `invoiceMatchesEntry` requires the invoice to be `stakeMsat` exactly.

Checking `feeMsat` therefore needs, in this order:
  1. A RULING on which section stands. Under 18, `feeMsat` should be 2% of that
     entry's `stakeMsat`. Under 22A Collection, `stakeMsat` is already net and
     `feeMsat` is 2% of a commitment the Entry Contract does not carry - which
     would need a new signed field before the check is even expressible.
  2. Only then, whether the RATE belongs in the round contract. If 2% is fixed
     by 22A for everyone - "2%, identical for everyone" - it is a constant like
     `SLASH_TO_PLAYERS_BPS` and no field is needed. A field would let an
     operator price its own round's fee, which is the fault contract fields
     exist to prevent.

Nothing was patched to hide this, and the contract was not touched.

## M2.1 22A: an entry's fee, checked against its own stake

18 stands, ruled: fees ride ON TOP of the stake and do not reduce the pool, so
`stakeMsat` is the gross stake and 2% of it is what the player was charged
beside it. 22A's Collection clause - a 100 sat commitment giving a 96 sat net
stake - contradicts 18 and 22A's own worked example, and is treated as the
error. No commitment field was added and the round contract was not touched.

THE RATE STAYS A CONSTANT. 22A calls it "2%, identical for everyone", so one
rate covers every entry of every round. A contract field would let an operator
price its own round's fee, which is the fault a contract field exists to
prevent rather than one to import - the same shape as a caller argument that
should have been a signed number, read the other way round.

### What went in

`entryFeeMsat(stakeMsat)` - 2% with the same integer floor `nodeFeeTable`
already uses, so one rate is applied one way - and `feeMatchesEntry(entry)`,
which answers rather than throws, like every other decision in this package.

  charged 2000 of 100000   stands
  charged 2001             does not: "the 1 over is money no fee table
                           allocates"
  charged 1999             does not
  charged 0 on a stake     does not
  malformed or negative    answered, not thrown

TOO MUCH IS THE DIRECTION THAT BECOMES INCOME, and that is why the refusal is
worded from it. The fee table computes from the STAKES, so an entry charged
9999 where 2% is 2000 leaves 7999 that the table allocates to nobody -
measured: `gross` 100000, `fee` 2000, and paid plus unallocated 2000. The
excess simply stays with whoever collected it, which is the operator.

### The floor does not aggregate, measured and not reconciled

Each entry pays `floor(2% of its own stake)`; the table owes
`floor(2% of the sum)`. These are different numbers:

| round | collected per entry | table owes | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 x 149 msat | 4 | 5 | 1 |
| 7 x 33333 msat | 4662 | 4666 | 4 |
| 3 x 49 msat | 0 | 2 | 2 |
| 61 x 100000 msat (22A's example) | 122000 | 122000 | 0 |

The gap is at most one millisatoshi per entry and ALWAYS in the same
direction - collected <= owed - so it can never become income. It is recorded
rather than patched: 22A defines the fee on the gross and says nothing about
which rounding a collector uses, and picking one here would be inventing a
rule. The spec's own worked example is one of the cases that agrees exactly.

| a fee of nothing is accepted | 1 |
| a malformed entry throws at the caller | 1 |
| negative money is money | 1 |
| the fee is measured against the whole round | 1 |

## M2.1 22A: the donation, split and never redirected

`donationMsat` has been on every Entry Contract since it was written and was
read by NOTHING - measured with the same grep that found `feeMsat` unread a
turn earlier. This is the arithmetic and the one rule that says where the money
does not go when a payment fails.

### The rounding here is not the fee's rounding

22A gives the node fee's remainder to ascending `H(round_id || node_pubkey)`
and gives the donation's to "the first recipient in the set AS PUBLISHED.
Deterministic, and the amounts are too small for anything cleverer to be worth
its complexity." Two rules, written separately in one section; copying either
onto the other would be inventing a third. Two mutants pin it: sending the
remainder to the last recipient, and sending it to the biggest share, are 1 red
each.

### What went in

`packages/protocol/src/donation.js`, on the money guard, which is 12 files now.

  the set stands      only when the shares sum to EXACTLY 10000 basis points.
                      Under anything else money is either left over with nobody
                      named to receive it or promised twice, and 22A says MUST.
                      9999 and 10001 are both refused by name.
  one party, one      the same `lnurl` twice is refused. The set is meant to be
  share               "a parameter the network can hold an opinion about", and
                      it cannot form one if an address appears under two
                      weights.
  the split is EXACT  floor each share, remainder to the first as published, so
                      the shares sum to the donation to the millisatoshi.
                      Measured over 1, 3, 7, 999, 2001, 100003 and 999999999
                      msat. That is a different property from the node fee,
                      where each entry's own floor can collect less than the
                      round's table owes - here there is no gap for anybody to
                      keep.
  donations off       pay nothing, and 22A says the set is IRRELEVANT to that
                      entry, so a zero donation is answered without judging the
                      set at all - even a set that would not stand.

Measured, and one expectation of mine was wrong on the way: 2001 msat over
3333/3333/3334 is 668/666/667, and REVERSED it is 669/666/666 rather than the
668 I had written. Reversing puts the 3334 share first, so its own floor is 667
and the same two left over make 669. The order decides who is topped up; the
share decides what they are topped up from. Corrected against the arithmetic.

### The clause this exists for

22A: clients "MUST NOT redirect the share to the remaining recipients, which
would let one unreachable endpoint quietly redistribute other people's money."

  one of three fails   the other two are paid exactly what they were owed
                       before - 668 and 667 of a 2001 donation - and the 666
                       simply does not move
  all three fail       nobody is paid, 2001 unpaid
  either way           the entry STANDS: a donation is voluntary and outside
                       the pool, so a failure can neither void a round nor
                       touch a stake

It is the money-law clause and not a retry policy: whether a client tries again
is its business, and where the money may go is not.

### Deliberately not here

22A also says the set "is named in the Round Contract and its hash is part of
the contract hash". That is a signed field and it moves every round id - the
same split the fee table took before `feeMsat`, and it is a decision before it
is work. And there is no Lightning in this package: a recipient is an opaque
`lnurl` string, because inventing a payment layer to test one would be
inventing a second protocol.

## M2.1 22A: the donation set becomes bytes a committee can check

The hole was named in the follow-up before it was coded: `donation.js` had no
encoder, no tagged hash and no id - measured, `grep` for `encode`, `Id` or
`taggedHash` in that file returned nothing - so a recipient set was a
JavaScript array living in one process. Every other object here that decides
money carries a tagged id precisely so a stranger can re-derive it: the payout
table, the settlement record, the fee claim, the service record, the slash
proof. The donation set was the only one that did not, and that is what stopped
two independent nodes agreeing on WHICH set a player donated under.

`TYPE_DONATION_SET = 0x10` and `BLWP/v1/DonationSet`, next free number, the
same pattern the fee claim and service record used.

### The order is part of the set, and is deliberately NOT sorted

This is the one place in the package where a vector is left unsorted, and it is
the opposite of a slip. Everywhere else sorting is what makes two honest
callers agree - the payout table by pubkey, the committee by key - and here it
would hide a real difference in who gets paid: 22A gives the remainder to "the
first recipient in the set AS PUBLISHED", so a reordered set pays somebody else
the odd millisatoshi and must be a different set with a different id.

  set as published        d201913a094e5b6d...
  the same three reversed abca72ffcef40139...

The mutant that sorts the recipients - which would make those two ids equal -
is 1 red.

### A set that does not stand has no id at all

Refused at the encoder AND at the decoder. Without the first there would be
bytes carrying a real tagged id over shares summing to 9999: an object as
published-looking as an honest one that hands out a different amount than the
player chose. Without the second a stranger's bytes would be trusted, and a
stranger is exactly who might send a set that does not stand - measured with a
tampered byte that turns 5000 into 4999.

### The zero-donation answer is `owed`, not `ok`

22A says the set is irrelevant to an entry that donates nothing, so a zero
donation succeeds even against a set that would NOT stand. A field called `ok`
invited a caller to read that as "this set stands", which it never said. `owed`
says what the function answers - what each recipient is owed - and whether a
set stands is `donationSetStands`, a different question with a different name.
The arithmetic did not change. A test asserts `'ok' in` the answer is false, so
the old reading cannot come back quietly; the mutant that adds `ok` back is
1 red.

### Parked, with the reason stated

`failed` is a caller-supplied list of `lnurl`s. Nothing in this package can
verify that a Lightning payment failed - there is no Lightning here, the same
way there is no curve - so it is an attestation of the same class as
`replayDiffers` and 5A.3B's own residual. Not implemented behind a guess.

The set is still NOT on the round contract. 22A wants it hashed into the
contract hash, and that moves every round id: a decision before it is work, the
same split the fee table took before `feeMsat`. What this turn adds is the
hash, which has to exist before anything can carry it.

| the set is sorted, so reorder is the same set | 1 |
| bytes that do not stand decode anyway | 1 |
| trailing bytes are ignored | 1 |
| the zero-donation flag is `ok` again | 1 |

## M2.1 22A: an LNURL is bech32, and its case rules are bech32's

A defect in the check delivered one commit earlier, found by auditing it rather
than by a test. `donationSetStands` compared `lnurl` by exact string equality,
so measured on the delivered code:

    [{LNURL1ABC, 5000}, {lnurl1abc, 5000}]  ->  STANDS, id 6b847471c97e87d2

That is ONE PARTY HOLDING TWO SHARES - exactly what the duplicate check exists
to prevent - and the same payee produced two different set ids
(`e8b941be2898bcdf` upper against `e9173b82ff008c57` lower), so two honest
nodes handed the same recipients in different case disagreed about which set
was used.

### The rules are the encoding's, not this file's

Bech32 says a string may not be mixed case, and that case carries no meaning.
Both are now enforced: a mixed-case address does not stand, identity is
compared canonically, and the bytes carry the canonical form so the id follows.

    two spellings of one payee   refused, "one party with two shares"
    LnUrL1abc                    refused, "mixed case, which bech32 does not allow"
    all-upper id                 4ea755742786f087
    all-lower id                 4ea755742786f087   (the same set)

### Folded in ASCII, and not with `toLowerCase`

`toLowerCase` is Unicode: in a Turkish locale it maps `I` to a dotless `ı`, so
two implementations of this protocol could canonicalise one address two
different ways and disagree about who is being paid. Bech32 is ASCII, so the
fold is ASCII - `A`-`Z` only, and `İ` and `Ä` are left exactly as they are. The
mutant that swaps the fold for `toLowerCase` is 1 red.

### Nothing published in lowercase moved

VERIFIED AGAINST THE PRE-FOLD CODE ITSELF rather than reasoned about: the
previous `donation.js` was checked out beside the new one and both were asked
for the id of an all-lower set. Both answer **44022895c61f07fd**. Lowercase was
already what the fold outputs, so those bytes never moved. A set typed in UPPER
does change id - to the id its lowercase twin already had - which is the point
of the ruling.

A test that guessed a number was corrected here too: I first wrote a
placeholder id into that assertion and called it measured. It was not. The
number above is the one both versions actually produce.

### Round-trip is canonical, and says so

`decodeDonationSet(encodeDonationSet(upperSet))` returns the lowered form, so
the round-trip assertion compares against the canonical set rather than the
input. That is the behaviour, not a weakened test: the payee is the same payee
either way, and the bytes say which payee.

| the fold uppercases instead | 2 |
| nothing is mixed case | 2 |
| duplicates are compared verbatim again | 1 |
| mixed case stands | 1 |
| the fold is Unicode, not ASCII | 1 |

## M2.1 22A: one set, one byte string - the last of the payee-identity defect

Found auditing the fold that had just been delivered, not by a test.

THE ENCODER FOLDS, SO NOTHING THIS PACKAGE WRITES IS EVER UPPERCASE - measured,
`encodeDonationSet` typed in either case emits the same bytes. But a stranger
does not use this encoder. Hand-crafted bytes spelling the payee `LNURL1ABC`
decoded happily and stood:

    canonical bytes   100001000100096c6e75726c3161...   (lnurl1abc)
    hand-crafted      100001000100094c4e55524c3141...   (LNURL1ABC)
    both decoded, both stood

One set with two byte strings. A committee comparing what it received - or
hashing it directly instead of re-encoding - would see two different sets and
disagree, which is exactly the disagreement folding was adopted to remove. The
id was only canonical because `donationSetId` re-encodes; anyone hashing the
wire bytes got the other answer, `e9173b82ff008c57`.

The decoder refuses them now. REFUSED RATHER THAN QUIETLY FOLDED ON THE WAY IN:
bytes that are not the set's own encoding are not that set, and folding them
would make the id depend on who did the hashing. Both mutants die - accepting
them, and folding instead of refusing, 1 red each.

Our own upper-typed set still round-trips: `encodeDonationSet` lowers it, and
`decodeDonationSet` returns `lnurl1abc`. Nothing an honest caller does changed.

Hole B, the last unblocked thing in sub-item 3. 22A: "The set is named in the
Round Contract and its HASH IS PART OF THE CONTRACT HASH, so it cannot change

## M2.1 22A: the set is bound but its bytes are not published - a recorded limit

A round binds `donationSetId` inside the Round Contract and therefore inside
the round id, so an entry cannot stand under a set the contract did not name
and a set cannot change after entry. NOTHING PUBLISHES THE PREIMAGE: a verifier
can say WHICH set a round bound and cannot fetch its recipients.

That is the same shape as a transcript whose inputs were never published - §11
already has that limit, and §13C's canonical transcript refuses a mark
committing to inputs the object does not carry for exactly this reason. 22A
names no channel for the set, and inventing one - gossip, a fetch endpoint, a
preimage API - would be inventing a second protocol, so none was added.

WHAT IT DOES NOT WEAKEN. The binding stands on its own: a set that does not
stand has no id at all, a set that is not the round's is refused by name, and
the round id moved to prove the hash includes it. What the limit costs is the
ability to CHECK A SPLIT, which nothing does today - the client pays the
donation outside the pool, no node touches it, and `failed` is already a parked
attestation because this package has no Lightning.

Parked beside the other data-availability limits, not counted as a hole in the
binding.

## Working order: why stage 5 is next and stage 4 is not

Read off IMPLEMENTATION.md rather than chosen. Its build order gives stage 4 as
"Replay pool, result signing, 5-of-7 finality, objection window, equivocation,
no-quorum" - and everything in that line except the replay pool is already in:
result signing, 5-of-7 finality, the objection window, both limbs of 13B and
13C's no-quorum outcome. The leftover REPLAY POOL is the committee re-run,
which is parked, and parked for a reason this repo enforces rather than
inherits: the daemon imports no core and does not step, so a replay pool inside
it is the second simulator the whole design exists to avoid.

So the next stage that is not one of the five parked items is stage 5:

    | 5 | Chain integration: bond verification, census build, committee
        publication, timestamp receipts | A contract with a wrong census root
        is rejected by every node |

Some of it already exists and that is worth naming before anyone starts:
`chain.js` and `tx.js` verify a bond into a mined chain and `census.js` has
`buildCensus`. What is absent is the part the "done when" is written around -
every node deriving the same census from the chain, so a contract that names a
root nobody else computes is refused rather than played.

The list now carries it as item 15, NOT STARTED, above 14 because 14's own
remainder is blocked - not because 14 is finished. Item 14 stays OPEN.

## M2.2 5A.4: a contract's census root is checked against the census it names

The first slice of item 15, and the cut was changed before it was built: the
letter's original slice bundled "same chain -> same census root" with "a wrong
root is refused". Those cost very different things. Refusing a wrong root needs
NOTHING new - the derivation was already here. "Same chain" needs 5A.4's SCAN
step, and 5A.3B is blunt that a light client cannot be handed a proof of
unspentness at all. So the slice built is the second half alone.

### Measured before writing anything

`censusRoot` was named by every Round Contract and read by NO CODE - `grep`
found it only in `contracts.js`, and nothing called `buildCensus` outside the
tests and the vector tool. A round could name any thirty-two bytes and be
played, which makes the committee whatever the round's author said it was.

Against 5A.4's five steps: SORT is done and done the spec's way (by
`(funding_txid, vout)`, not the grindable `H(node_pubkey)` v4.6 had); COMMIT is
nearly done; FILTER applies height, confirmations and unspent but not the bond
template, `bond_min(role)`, the advert signature or the declared role; RESOLVE
has the hash-matching half; SCAN is absent. **One of five complete, one nearly,
three partial or absent - and the check that ties a contract to any of it was
0 of 1.**

### What went in

`censusRootMatchesRound(contract, { entries, minConfirmations, tipHeight,
boundTo })`. The height comes off the CONTRACT, not the asker: recomputing at
another height is recomputing a different census, and a caller who could choose
it could make an honest contract look wrong.

`censusInputsId` binds the set, the height and the depth rule, the same
discipline `payoutInputsId` needed for 5A.3 row 3 - a root is a function of a
SET, so a caller free to choose the set can make any honest contract look wrong
by handing in a different list. Sorted by outpoint, the census's own rule, so
the order a node happened to receive entries in does not move the commitment.

  same entries, either order    one root, 73df1096be9eedf1... over 3 entries
  the root its census derives   playable
  a flipped bit, zeroes, or
    another set's root          refused, and the refusal NAMES `censusRoot`
                                and says what the root should have been
  a swapped or shortened set    refused: "not the census entries that were
                                published"
  a changed depth rule          same refusal - the commitment covers it
  a duplicate outpoint          refused with `buildCensus`'s own reason, not
                                thrown at whoever asked whether a round is
                                playable

### Two signed-shape divergences, recorded and NOT fixed

  1. The census leaf carries `pubkey`; 5A.4 says the canonical serialization is
     `outpoint || advertisement hash || bond_amount || role bits`. Changing it
     moves every census root and the census vector.
  2. The Round Contract carries ONE `censusRoot`; 5A.4 says `census_root[role]`
     - one per role pool. A second field is another round-id move.

Both are decisions before they are work, and neither was slipped in under a
slice about checking a root.

### Mutants: 13 planted, 13 killed, none retracted

| mutant | protocol red |
|--------|-------------:|

protocol 283/283 (was 275), blwp-node 70/70, blwp-client 89/89, core 80/80,

## M2.2 5A.4 step 1: SCAN reads the chain instead of believing the entry

**SCAN accounts for 1 of the 3 that is still missing for census from chain.**
Of 5A.4's five steps, SORT and COMMIT are done; SCAN, RESOLVE and FILTER
remain. Within SCAN, **3 of its 4 conjuncts are buildable and the fourth is
not.**

### What was already believed, and now is not

`buildCensus` applied "created at or before census_height", "unspent" and
"minimum depth" all along - to FIELDS THE CALLER SUPPLIED. A census was a bag
of entries somebody asserted heights and spends for. `scanCensus` reads both
off the blocks, so a publisher who lies about either is caught by anyone
holding the same chain. Measured: entries whose `height` and `spent` claim
`1` and `true` come back with the chain's own values.

### The fourth conjunct, and its blocker is not a daemon

"whose script matches the bond template (5A.3B)" is a FINDING operation, and
finding a bond needs `BOND_MARKER` - 25.1's single dust address that puts every
bond into the compact filters. `BOND_MARKER` is `null` in this protocol by a
decision already recorded in `constants.js`: it is a genesis parameter, fixed
once before the first bond exists, and "writing a plausible address into this
file would be settling it by accident in a source tree". `bondMarker()` throws
saying so, and a test asserts both.

So the candidate outpoints come IN, from the advertisements a node already
holds, which name `bondTxid` and `bondVout`. Enumerating from the chain alone
waits on that parameter - **not** on a daemon, and not on anything a fixture
could stand in for. That is a third kind of blocker beside the daemon, the tick
rate and the discrete-log group, and it is named rather than worked around: a
scanner that guessed which taproot outputs were bonds would be inventing the
discovery rule 25.1 exists to fix.

### Measured on recorded blocks, no daemon anywhere

  heights            read off the blocks; a claimed height is ignored
  spends             read off the blocks; a claimed spend is ignored
  the census block   INCLUDED - "at or before census_height"
  a later block      not read at all: a block after the census is one the
                     census did not see, and reading it would make the answer
                     depend on when a node asked
  a spend after the
    census height    does not retire the bond
  depth              a bond 3 deep at a tip is out where one 13 deep is in
  an unknown
    outpoint         NAMED in `missing`, not dropped - a census that quietly
                     lost a bond and one that never had it look identical from
                     the root alone
  end to end         a scanned census satisfies the contract's root, and the
                     same contract against a chain where one bond was spent
                     does not

### Mutants: 15 planted, 15 killed, none retracted

Two survived at 0 red first, and both were gaps in my fixtures rather than in
the code:

  - "blocks at the census height are skipped" - every block in the fixture was
    strictly earlier than the census, so `>` and `>=` were indistinguishable. A
    census could have silently dropped every bond funded in its own block. A
    block at exactly `censusHeight` went in; the mutant then dies at 1.
  - "outputs are indexed under the wrong key" - every candidate sat at vout 0,
    so indexing every output under `:0` looked correct and a bond at vout 1
    would have been read as the output beside it. A vout-1 candidate, a
    vout-9 miss and a both-vouts case went in; that mutant dies at 1 and
    dropping the vout from the key dies at 8.

The rest: blocks after the height read 2, the claimed height believed 4, the
claimed spend believed 3, nothing ever spent 2, an unknown outpoint invented 2,
one silently dropped 2, and the three input refusals 1 each.

## M2.2 5A.4 step 2: RESOLVE, and the three 5A.3 filters that wait on nothing

**This accounts for 3 of the 6 that was still missing for census from chain.**
5A.3 lists six eligibility criteria; "bond exists, unspent, deep enough" was
already done by SCAN. Of the six that remained:

  RESOLVE - body retrievable and hash-matching   THIS SLICE
  bond_amount >= bond_min(role)                  THIS SLICE
  declares the role and a supported version      THIS SLICE
  bond output uses the bond script template      BLOCKED - a taproot output
                                                 hides its script paths until
                                                 spent (5A.3B), the same wall
                                                 BOND_MARKER stands behind
  advertisement signature under node_pubkey      PARKED - no curve here, the
                                                 standing package boundary
  SCAN's finding conjunct                        BLOCKED - BOND_MARKER is null

So the three built are exactly the three needing neither a genesis parameter,
a curve, nor a daemon. **Item 15's remaining conjuncts are those three.**

### RESOLVE does not re-prove inclusion, and that is deliberate

`acceptAdvert` bundles a merkle proof with the resolution, because it is used
where nothing has established the transaction is in the chain. SCAN has - it
read the blocks. Demanding a header and a branch again would make RESOLVE ask
for what step 1 already answered, and 5A.4 asks something narrower of it: read
the committed hash, retrieve the body, match. So the resolution is done from
the transaction alone, with the same primitives.

### Three holes the tests found, each by failing honestly

  1. A DIFFERENT BUT SELF-CONSISTENT TRANSACTION RESOLVED HAPPILY. Handing back
     another node's bond worked, because a coherent transaction commits to its
     own body - so an entry at one outpoint could be resolved with an
     advertisement from somewhere else entirely, endpoint and all. The
     transaction must be the one the outpoint names. Found by a test that
     failed rather than by a mutant.
  2. An uncommitted witness body would have been taken if the check were
     dropped, because every transaction this repo builds commits to its own.
     A bond whose OP_RETURN names something else went in - `bondTransaction`
     already takes a `commitment` override - and that mutant now dies.
  3. A transaction committing to NOTHING was never tested, because every
     transaction here carries an OP_RETURN. Rather than fabricate one, the
     real mainnet block-100000 transaction already in `tx.test.js` was used:
     pre-segwit, two P2PKH outputs, no commitment.

And a fourth: THE RESOLVED BODY WINS OVER THE ENTRY'S SUMMARY. The roles in a
census row are somebody's transcription; the body is what the bond committed
to. A census that believed the transcription would let a publisher put a node
in a role its own advertisement never claimed. Tested with an entry claiming
`settlement` against an advertisement declaring `game`.

### Measured

  every body resolves            3 of 3 eligible, and the endpoint comes off
                                 the resolved body
  one body unreachable           excluded, named; the census is not broken
  a resolver that THROWS         the same - a failing peer is a failed
                                 retrieval, not an exception for the caller
  a bond of 49999 at a floor
    of 50000                     out, and the SAME bond is in a round whose
                                 floor is 10000: "the network stratifies; it
                                 does not evict"
  exactly the floor              in - 5A.3 says >=
  no role declared               out
  version 99 against ours        out; 99 AND ours is in
  what it cannot check           returned in `unchecked`, both named

### Mutants: 14 planted, 14 killed, none retracted

Three survived at 0 red first and all three were gaps in the fixtures, closed
as described above. The rest: any transaction resolving any entry 1, an
unretrievable body kept 1, a throwing resolver breaking the census 1, the floor
not applied / excluding the exact floor / being a constant 1 each, a role not
needed 1, any version supported 1, no floor or no resolver needed 1 each, and
the unchecked list emptied 1.

## M2.2 the five steps become one derivation, and the leaf names the advertisement

Found by re-reading the slice above rather than by a failing test: the five
steps of 5A.4 never joined, and the parts were reachable in the wrong order.

  - `scanCensus` returned a `census` field of its own. That root was taken
    with steps 2 and 3 UNRUN, so the shortest path through this package
    produced a census over nodes whose advertisements nobody had read.
    RESOLVE was a thing a caller might remember to do.
  - RESOLVE overrode the entry's ROLES with the advertisement's and left its
    PUBKEY alone. The leaf hashes the pubkey. So a census could name a key
    that never bonded - and the committee seed, the receipts and the payout
    table all read that key afterwards. Same hole as the roles one, one field
    over, and the field that matters more. I fixed the field a test pointed
    at instead of the class.

### What is now true

  deriveCensus   SCAN -> RESOLVE -> FILTER -> SORT -> COMMIT, one call, and
                 the only function that ends in a root.
  commitCensus   steps 4 and 5, and it REFUSES an entry with no advertisement
                 id: "that entry has not been resolved". Not a flag - the id
                 is the hash the bond output committed to, which only step 2
                 can find. So no root over unresolved nodes from any door,
                 including `censusRootMatchesRound`.
  scanCensus     applies its own three conjuncts (created at or before the
                 height, unspent there, deep enough) and returns
                 `{entries, excluded}`. No root. It used to hand its findings
                 to the commit step and let that filter, which made SCAN a
                 lookup and put the rules in the wrong place.

5A.4 wants the advertisement hash IN the leaf, where this leaf still carries a
pubkey. That divergence is recorded below and not fixed, because it moves every
census root. Requiring the hash to be KNOWN costs nothing and moves nothing.

### The measurement asked for: candidate says X, advertisement says Y

  candidate pubkey X          ee ee ee ee ...
  advertisement key  Y        11 11 11 11 ...
  census entry key            11 11 11 11 ...   <- Y
  root, candidate lying       31199edecf53b8bc4617a97022e195a0946c6aa3...
  root, candidate honest      31199edecf53b8bc4617a97022e195a0946c6aa3...   IDENTICAL
  the leaf a root over X
    would have carried        761c34cec2d278abca1912dc2136336f3db3b456...

A wrong transcription does not move the root by one bit, and the leaf the
transcription would have produced is a different leaf. Both halves matter: the
first says the lie is inert, the second says the override is load-bearing.

### Mutants: 19 planted, 19 killed, none retracted

Three survived at 0 red first, and all three were real gaps:

  the resolution guard accepts any length   nothing handed it a 16-byte "id".
                                            A hash is 32 bytes; 16 is not a
                                            short id, it is not an id.
  the depth rule is off by one              the fixture was 3 deep and 13 deep
                                            against a floor of 6 - nothing sat
                                            on the line. Now a bond EXACTLY
                                            census_confirmations deep is in and
                                            one short is out, which is what
                                            ">=" says.
  resolveBody hands back no advertisement
    id                                      nothing checked WHICH id RESOLVE
                                            passed on, so a placeholder would
                                            have satisfied the guard and the
                                            derivation would have claimed a
                                            resolution it never did.

The other sixteen died first time: the pubkey override dropped (1), the entry's
key kept when the advert has one (1), the guard removed entirely (1), scan
handing back a root again (1), scan not dropping a spent output (2), the depth
rule disabled (2) or unnamed in its reason (2), derive committing the SCANNED
entries (10), losing what scan dropped (1), losing what resolve dropped (1),
not saying which step dropped whom (1), swallowing a failed commit (1),
ignoring a refused resolve (1), refusing without a reason (1), not sorting (6),
and naming nothing it cannot check (1).
