## M2.2 item 20, second slice: the standing an interest set uses is the board's

`interestSet` read `rank` straight off the object it was handed. That is the
fault removed five times before - from the census depth, the committee size,
the committee seed, the bond floor and the protocol version. A rank a caller
picks is a rank the OPERATOR picks: say the player about to overtake you is
nineteenth and they fall out of the twenty you are shown, with nothing forged
and nothing to notice.

### What is now true

`interestSet(viewer, others, { limit, board })`. `others` carry a
`playerPubkey`; the standing is looked up on the BOARD by that key, and a
`rank` written on the caller's object is IGNORED - the treatment RESOLVE gives
a census entry's claimed roles and key, because the object is somebody's
summary and the signed thing beside it is what counts.

  the real leaders demoted to 900+ and the stragglers promoted to 0 on the
    caller's own objects   ->  the same set, unchanged
  no board at all          ->  no leaders at all; the whole budget goes to the
                               nearest, because nobody has a standing to be a
                               leader by

SOMEBODY STILL DRIVING HAS NO STANDING, and that is not a gap. A board is built
from results the committee has made final; mid-round most players have none.
They are watchable as neighbours and join the leaders half when their result is
final - and late join is why finals arrive DURING a round at all, since each
entrant gets T_run from their own start and they finish at different moments.

A REFUND IS NOT A STANDING either. The board shows it unranked, and unranked is
not a place.

### Mutants: 6 planted, 6 killed

Two survived at 0 red first, and both were fixtures that could not tell the
answers apart:

  a refund counts as a standing     the refunded players were placed NEAR, so
                                    the nearest half took them anyway and a
                                    leaders half that mistook `rank: null` for
                                    a standing looked identical. They are far
                                    away now and the unranked four are close,
                                    so the two halves disagree about them.
  the standing is keyed by entry,
    not by player                   every fixture used the same bytes for
                                    `entryId` and `playerPubkey`, so a lookup
                                    on either found the same row. They differ
                                    now, and the board's number one is placed
                                    FARTHEST away - a correct lookup gives it
                                    the leaders seat, a wrong one leaves the
                                    leaders half empty and the top of the board
                                    disappears.

The board fixture is built by calling `leaderboard` on real signed finals
rather than writing rank numbers by hand: hand-written ranks would test this
file against itself, and the point of the slice is that ONE ordering is
computed the same way everywhere.

TWO GAPS, both closed on the same slice.

A LEAKED NAMESPACE. `whose()` read `o.playerPubkey || o.entryId`. A board keys
by PLAYER and a subscription keys by ENTRY; they are different namespaces, and

  an other with NO playerPubkey, on a board ranking its entryId bytes
    before  ->  [5, 6]   the keyless truck took the leaders seat
    after   ->  [6, 7]   the seats go to the nearest, and the same truck WITH

  mutants   2 planted, 2 killed, 1 retracted with the code simplified
  protocol  375 -> 377

### The board's cost per broadcast, named not fixed

`standings(board)` rebuilds its map inside every `interestSet` call, so a
`fanOut` over N viewers rebuilds it N times - O(N.B) where B is the board. It
is correct and it is not free. Not changed here: the shape that fixes it is
hoisting the map into `fanOut`, which is a different slice and would be
measured against a real N rather than guessed at.

## M2.2 item 20, third slice: the payout on each row is the table's

Section 20 makes the payout table `F(contract, membership, results)`, and 0.11
makes the board presentation. A second thing that produced amounts would be a
second scoring path.

### The board is not handed a table

There is no argument for one. It is handed the INPUTS - the entries with their
stakes and outcomes - and calls `computePayoutTable`, the one implementation.
A forged table cannot be passed because there is nowhere to pass it, which is
the same shape as the core's missing ghost parameter: the guarantee is the
absence, not a check.

AND THE INPUTS MUST BE THIS ROUND'S. Every payout entry is measured against the
final the board already accepted:

  a player the committee made no final for   "counts a player the committee has
                                              made no result final for"
  FAILED promoted to DELIVERED               "says DELIVERED for a player whose
                                              final result is FAILED"
  a score inflated to 9999                   "scores a player 9999 where the
                                              final says 800"
  an amountMsat written on the input          ignored - the board reads the
                                              table it computed, exactly as an
                                              injected rank is ignored

### Zero is a paid amount

The table lists everybody activated, and a qualifier who places outside the
paying ranks is paid 0n. A player the table does not list at all - a refunded
run, which section 18 says neither contributes nor draws - has NO `payoutMsat`
field. Measured both ways in one board: the loser carries `payoutMsat: 0n` and
`'payoutMsat' in row` is true; the refunded player has no such key.

### Payout is a column, not a sort key

The order was settled by score then player key; money must not move anybody.
The mutant that sorted by amount survived at first because the fixture's payout
order agreed with its score order - the fourth time this letter a fixture could
not tell two answers apart. It is measured on a CROSSED pair now: a FAILED run
with the highest score is ranked first and paid nothing, while a lower-scoring
delivery is ranked second and paid.

the board computing an amount itself (2 red), an amount read off the caller's
object (3), a player the table omits paid zero (1), a payout entry not matched
to the final outcome (1) or the final score (1), a player with no final paid
(1), and payout used as a sort key (1).

### The bookkeeping first

PRIORITIES said of slice 1 "and no column carries money" while slice 3, two

contradicts itself in adjacent sentences is read at the top of every turn.

### The hole

`provisionallyFinal` counts `{ resultId, nodePubkey }` pairs against the
round's committee. It does NOT verify a signature, and `result.js` says why:
"this package carries no curve, so the caller passes what it has checked."
That boundary is right.

What was wrong is that the BOARD did not say so. Five entries in an array were
counted as five committee signatures and the answer came back looking exactly
like a verified one. Every other door names its curve boundary - `resolveCensus`

    2. pseudonym

    4. live run status

`signaturesVerified` is a claim about the CALLER's own work, not about the
data, so it moves the report and nothing else: same rows, same order, same

## Item 20, slices 6 and 7: one round's board, one final per player

Both found by reading the board's own source, not by a failing test. `grep -n
roundId src/leaderboard.js` returned four hits, all inside comments: every
signed final carries `roundId` (contracts.js:243/260), the contract has a
computable id (contracts.js:191), and the board compared neither. There was no
duplicate-key check either - `payoutsFor`'s `byKey` collapses duplicates for
the TABLE, which is not the row loop.

### Slice 6, before and after

  BEFORE  3 finals of this round + 2 finals of another, same committee
          -> 5 rows, ranks 1..5, the foreign 800 sitting second
  AFTER   -> 3 rows, ranks 1..3, identical to the board this round's
             finals build alone; 2 exclusions named "final for a different
             round than this contract"

The foreign player is ABSENT, not paid nothing: a payout that counts them is
refused outright ("counts a player the committee has made no result final
for"), because there is no final in this round to check the entry against.

The id is COMPUTED. `roundId(contract)` hashes the encoded contract, so a
`roundId` field written on the contract object is ignored - measured, N2 below.
A contract that cannot be hashed refuses to build a board at all, rather than
building one that cannot say which round it is of.

### Slice 7, before and after

  BEFORE  [A 900, B 800, A 900, C 700] -> 4 rows, A twice, C at rank 4
  AFTER   -> 3 rows, C at rank 3, one exclusion "handed in more than once"

  BEFORE  [A 900, B 800, C 700, A 950] -> A shown twice, at 1 and at 2
  AFTER   -> A absent, B and C only, one exclusion "two different results are
             final for that player, and the board is not the place to choose
             between them"

A repeat and a contradiction are different things and are told apart by the
result id. The contradiction shows NEITHER: picking the higher score lets
whoever obtained a second signature set choose a rank, and picking the first
arrival lets arrival order choose it - the fault the whole file is built
against. Section 14 settles a conflict; a board does not.

## Item 21: the protocol tick is the core's TICK_DT, not sixty a second

The spec requires a "fixed protocol tick" (multiplayer_p2p.md:444, in the same
list as fixed-point arithmetic and canonical serialization) and names NO
number, no unit and no emitter. Ticks are only ever the unit something else is
counted in: a checkpoint's `tick` (10), `first_tick`/`last_tick` (11),
`join_tick`, "the exposure integral accumulated per simulation tick" (1711).
The contract measures the round in TIME - `start_time`, `entry_close_time`,
`player_run_duration // T_run`, worked example "T_run: 3 minutes". Nothing
converted, which is why 15's CLTV floor and 19's two clocks were parked.

### Where the number came from, and where it did not

  core/src/sim.js:103   const TICK_DT = 1092;   // private, not exported
  core/src/rules/air.js Y_LERP written against the TICK, not a sixtieth:
                        1-exp(-2/60) gave 2149 where the tick asks for 2148
  BlwpNet.cs            a comment saying 60 ticks a second - LEFT WHERE IT IS

The owner is the core: the tick is a property of the binary `simCoreHash`
commits to, so a round signed under one core cannot be replayed under another
and disagree about how long it was. A literal in the protocol would be a second
clock. Same shape as hash.js taking sha256bytes off the core.

### The measured numbers

  one tick            1092 / 65536 s = 0.01666259765625 s
  ticks per second    65536 / 1092 = 60.014652... - NO integer value exists
  60 ticks            65520 Q16.16 s, 16 short of a second
                      = 999 ms + 1548/2048 = 999.755859375 ms
  1000 ms             60 ticks + 500/34125 of a tick
  10,800 ticks        11,793,600 Q16.16 s = 179956 ms + 112/2048
                      = 179.9560546875 s - 44 ms SHORT of three minutes
  180,000 ms          10802 ticks + 21750/34125 of a tick
                      (rounding would give 10803: a tick nobody simulated)
  3,600,000 ms        216052 ticks + 25500/34125; back again 3599987 ms +
                      1124/2048, so the round trip loses 13 ms - under one tick

ms per tick is DERIVED, not typed: TICK_DT x 1000 / ONE, reduced by gcd to
34125/2048 at load. No third literal exists to drift from the other two.

### The shape of the conversion

  secondsQ16ForTicks  exact always - a tick IS TICK_DT of these units, so it
                      is a multiplication and nothing is lost
  msForTicks          floor + { remainder, divisor, exact }
  ticksForMs          FLOOR, never round + { remainder, divisor, exact }
  exactTicksForMs     REFUSES with the remainder in the reason

Floor and not round, because 10802.637 rounds to 10803 and a round whose last
tick exists only in the contract has a transcript one tick short - two honest
nodes disagreeing with nothing to arbitrate it. Negative durations throw:
floor and truncation part company below zero, and the answer is to refuse the
question rather than silently pick one.

### Mutants: 7 planted, 7 killed, 0 retracted

  P1 sixty ticks a second substituted for the ratio      5 red  (required)
  P2 ms -> ticks rounds instead of flooring              2 red  (required)
  P3 ticks -> ms rounds instead of flooring              2 red
  P4 the remainder dropped and `exact` always true       3 red
  P5 exactTicksForMs serves a guess instead of refusing  1 red
  P6 the core's TICK_DT moved to 1100                    5 red here, and 2 red
                                                         in core rules
  P7 the ratio left unreduced                            5 red

P6 is the pair the sequence asked to measure first. `test/rules.test.js:1185`
declared its OWN `const TICK_DT = 1092` - a copy, so sim.js could have moved to
1100 while the test went on checking 1092 against a constant written for 1092.
It now imports the core's export and asserts the value, so a moved tick fails
in the file that owns it and in the file that reads it. Y_LERP is unchanged at
2148: the pair measured the same before and after the export.

## Item 22, slices 4 and 5: the queue an objection cannot be flooded out of, and the signature

### The pool

Order is not arrival. 13A gives an objection a WINDOW, so first-come-first-
served is the one rule an attacker can use: flood a node with undisputed runs
the moment somebody objects and the objection is heard after the window shuts.
A veto that expires unheard was never there.

  the classes                objected, then the board's ranked, then the rest
                             (PRIORITIES 1427, the spec's own three)
  what the pool computes     neither: an objection is a fact the node holds and
                             a rank is letter 20's board. A pool that sorted
                             players would be a second leaderboard.

  MEASURED ORDER, one worker, submitted busy / plain-a / ranked / plain-b /
  objected:      busy, objected, ranked, plain-a, plain-b
  and with ten undisputed runs already queued when one objection arrives, the
  objection is served SECOND, not twelfth.

  What this costs, said out loud: a stream of objections starves the rest. That
  is the accepted trade - an objection has a deadline and an ordinary replay
  does not.

CAPACITY IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED, so `workers` defaults to ONE: a node that
has measured its own machine says so, and a node that has not gets the number
that cannot be wrong. Measured here: 36,000 ticks in one worker in 4141 ms =
8,694 ticks/s, 145x realtime. A three-minute run (10,802 ticks, letter 21) is
about 1.24 s of one worker.

There is NO argument for what does the replaying. It was going to take one so a
test could watch the order without starting threads; that is a hole, because a
caller who can hand in the replayer can hand in one that agrees with anything.
The order is watched through `pool.order` on real workers instead.

### The signature

Section 13 is explicit: each node replays and signs `PlayerResult { round_id,
player_pubkey, result, score, transcript_hash, sim_wasm_hash, node_pubkey,
signature }`, and five IDENTICAL ones are PROVISIONALLY_FINAL.

THERE IS NO SIGNED STATE-HASH OBJECT IN THE SPEC. `state_hash` appears once, on
the player's own Checkpoint (10). The obvious build - a little attestation
carrying the agreed hash - would have been a second protocol, two signed things
both saying what a run came to. So the agreement is signed as the result the
committee was always going to sign, and letter 20's board already counts
exactly these signatures. The state hash is WHY two nodes' ids match, not a
field beside them.

  outcome        read off the replayed state: the core ends a run LIVE,
                 DELIVERED, WRECKED or MISSED, and DELIVERED is the only one
                 that delivered; wrecked and missed are both FAILED, which is
                 the whole of the difference 18 pays on. FORFEIT, VOID and
                 ENTRY_VOID are facts about a stake or an entry and a replay
                 must never return one. A run still LIVE at the last stored
                 tick has NO outcome - calling that FAILED would score a lost
                 connection as a lost run.
  score          runScore off the same state. 230 for the fixture run.
  transcriptHash the canonical transcript's, which is what says WHICH run was
                 replayed.
  threshold      receiptsNeeded(contract.gameVerifySlots). Nothing in the file
                 knows that seven means five.

  SIGNATURE CASES MEASURED
    five of seven over one result id        final
    four of the same                        not final
    four on one result, one on another      not final (5 verified, 4 agreeing)
    a signature made with the wrong key     dropped as forged, not final
    one seat's signature listed twice       counted once, not final
    a stranger's perfectly good signature   not a seat, not final
    two slots, two signatures               final; one is not
    slots 5                                 refused, "no committee threshold"

A signature that does not verify never reaches the count. That is the part the
protocol package says it cannot do - "counted against the round's committee,
not verified: no curve in this package" - and this one has a curve.

The machinery was complete and nothing called it. Measured before: `grep` for

The close is the event section 13 waits for. The promises are deliberately not
awaited at the socket: the caller is told the round is shut, and the replays

A note for the next sweep: `blwp-client`'s own `npm test` is

## Item 22, the committee half: nodes fetch each other's results

Serving a result nobody fetches is a committee of one writing in a diary.
Measured before: `/results` answered and NOTHING asked - `verifiedFinal` was
called from a test file and from nowhere else.

### Two daemons, two identities, one contract

Both seats named by the contract; each daemon told where the other answers,
because a contract names a committee by KEY and a key is not an address (25.1
makes finding one discovery's job, not this letter's). Real sockets.

  after both closes, without any test calling gather
      the node that closed second already holds 2 records
  gather on each          fetched >= 1, kept 1, held 2, needed 2, verified 2,
                          final true on both
  asking again            held 2, kept 0 - one seat, one result
  a stranger in the seat  final false, strangers 1

AGREEMENT IS ON THE RUN, NOT ON THE BYTES. Section 13's PlayerResult carries
`node_pubkey`, so two seats that replayed the same run to the same answer
produce two DIFFERENT result ids - the record names who made it. Counting ids
would put every honest committee at one of seven forever. The tally key is
therefore the result with the signer removed: computed in `verdict.js`, never
signed and never sent, so it adds no object to the protocol. Measured: the two

A run replayed before its transcript was carried is not a failure, it is an

after the close now re-queues that run.

  the second seat receipts      1 result, hashed over the canonical transcript,

## Item 22: the hole in fetch, and the committee seed from a future beacon

### The hole, found and closed before the beacon

`#keepPeerResult` checked the record's ROUND and not its PLAYER, and a
PlayerResult names no entry. The store keys a result by (round, entry, signer),
so a record about another player of the same round, signed impeccably by a real
seat, would take that seat's row under this entry - and the seat's true record,
arriving later, would be IGNOREd as a duplicate. One peer could stop any seat's
real answer from ever being stored without forging a signature. The record's
player is now checked against the entry the node itself holds. Mutant W1
(the check removed) 1 red.

### The seed, 5A.5's own formula

    committee_seed = H(census_root_game_verify || census_root_settlement
                       || round_id || round_randomness)

  two nodes, one published hash     the same 32 bytes
  every input moves it              beacon, round id, and each root
  the two roots are ordered         not interchangeable
  the same seed, same committee     7 of 10 selected, identical both times
  a different beacon                a different committee - which is the whole
                                    point: grinding round_ids no longer picks
                                    the seats
  pinned value                      H(4,5,6,7 filled) =
                                    9c28512a7b662b84f5b49848bcb9bede9cb6fcac
                                    da35892687a3c996288ed336

The pinned value exists because every other assertion compares a seed with
another seat's seed, so a change that moved every seed alike - the roots
swapped, the tag renamed, the parts joined differently - would pass all of
them. Mutants X6 and X7 both survived at 0 red until it was added.

### "Published after round_id", and exactly how much of it can be proved

  at or below census_height   refused, "the creator held that chain state
                              when the round was made"
  census_height + 1           accepted, provenAfter = census_height
  no height at all            refused - "I do not know when this was
                              published" and "it was published late enough"
                              must never be the same answer
  a fractional height         refused

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE, said plainly rather than implied: the contract
carries `census_height` and nothing else about time, so a beacon ABOVE that
height still cannot be shown to postdate publication. 5A.5 ties the beacon to
`committee_time`, and this contract has no `committee_time` and no publication
height. The check refuses what it can prove and names what it cannot.

### TWO CONTRADICTIONS BETWEEN THE TREE AND 5A.5, neither invented away

  1. `committeeSeed` IS A CONTRACT FIELD (contracts.js:112), inside the bytes
     `roundId` hashes. 5A.5 derives the seed FROM `round_id`. The two cannot
     both hold: a seed inside the id that is computed from the id is circular.
     The spec's answer is that the contract commits to WHICH beacon round will
     be used (`randomness_rule`), not to a seed - so the field should be a rule
     and not a value. That is a contract-format change, the letter-16 class,
     and it is not made here.
  2. The contract carries ONE `censusRoot` where 5A.5 hashes TWO - game/verify
     and settlement. `committeeSeedFromBeacon` fills both positions from the
     one root and returns `rootsAreOne: true` rather than hashing 32 fewer
     bytes in silence.

Both are named because they are the difference between a seed that closes the
grinding attack and a seed that looks as though it does.

## Item 23, slice 1: the advertisement signature

5A.1 ends the body with "signature - by node_pubkey over all of the above" and
nothing checked it. `chain.js` said so in the list it returns with every bond:
"the advertisement signature (no curve in this package)".

  before   acceptAdvert accepts a bond whose body is signed by ANY key, and
           hands back BOND_UNCHECKED with the signature on it (2 entries)
  after    acceptSignedAdvert accepts only a body signed by the key it names,
           and its unchecked list is 1 entry - the script template, which a
           taproot output really does hide until it is spent

ed25519 under node_pubkey: the key that already signs this daemon's receipts
and results. No second curve. The BOND key stays secp256k1 and its link to the
body is the commitment H(advert), not this signature - one says "this body is
worth money", the other "this body is mine".

### The refusals, each by name

  another key         "that advertisement is not signed by <key>, the node it
                      names" - and the chain door accepts that same
                      transaction, which is why this one exists
  a different body    a good signature over another advertisement's id fails
                      the same way
  another transaction "names a different bond transaction" - the chain's own
                      reason, not dressed up as a signature failure
  no signature        an unsigned body is refused

### THE ZERO KEY SIGNS ITSELF, measured

    ed25519.verify(zeros64, anything, zeros32) === true

Zero decodes to a point of small order and the equation closes trivially. And
`tools/bond.js` fills an unsigned body with exactly 64 zero bytes, calling them
in its own comment "a signature that verifies under no key" - they verify under
one. So an advertisement naming the zero key and carrying no signature would
have passed this door as signed by the node it names, and had its endpoint
handed to a player. Both halves are now refused by name. Of 256 uniform keys
tried, none made `verify` throw, so the catch around it is defensive only.

  Z5 the body-only check always passing             1 red
  Z6 the zero key allowed                           1 red
  Z7 an empty signature allowed on a loose body     1 red

Z2 IS RETRACTED, not counted: it only differs when `ed25519.verify` throws, and
it does not throw for any 32-byte key tried - it returns false. The catch is
there for an input shape this curve does not produce, so the mutant measures an
unreachable line rather than the check.

## Item 23, slice 2: the census took a body nobody had signed

The close-out asked whether another accept path still takes an unsigned or
foreign-key advertisement. One did, and it was the one that matters most.

`census.js` RESOLVE split the signed body and threw the signature away -
literally `const { body } = splitSignedAdvert(bytes)` - so ELIGIBILITY rested
on a body that had been committed to and never authored, and the gap was named
in `unchecked` instead. Naming a gap is right while nothing can close it; it
stopped being right once a caller could.

The protocol package still carries no curve and must not: it is the one every
other package reads. So `verifyAdvert` is injected, the way `provesEquivocation`
takes one. With no verifier the behaviour is exactly as before - the body is
counted and the gap is named - so nothing that could not check is now pretending
to.

  without one          the same body is eligible and the signature is still
                       listed as unchecked
  the zero key         refused whatever the verifier says
  the empty signature  refused whatever the verifier says

Measured twice: with a stub verifier in the protocol package, which has no
curve, and with real ed25519 one package over, where the daemon's own key

## Item 24: the bond output key is the taproot tweak, not filler

### What was there

`tools/bond.js` posted `[0x51, 0x20, ...fill(0x77)]` - a P2TR output whose key
was derived from nothing, so every fixture bond was unfalsifiable and
`recognizeBond` could only say the output LOOKED like taproot. The last entry
of `BOND_UNCHECKED` said so: "the bond script template (5A.3B: a taproot output
hides it until spent)".

### Why recomputing is the only check there can be

A taproot output shows nothing until it is spent, which is exactly why 5A.3B
chose it - "a cooperative release and a cooperative slash are the same
transaction". So verification cannot READ the script. It rebuilds the tree from
what the node declares and asks whether the 32 bytes on chain are the answer.
Construction and verification are one function used twice.

### The shape, and where the curve is

  leaf A (recovery)  <node_key> CHECKSIGVERIFY <maturity> CLTV DROP
  leaf B (slash)     <k> <m sorted keys> <m> CHECKMULTISIG
  branch             BIP-341 TapBranch, children in lexicographic order
  tweak              TapTweak(internal_key || merkle_root)
  output key         Q = P + t*G, done by the CALLER's curve

The protocol package does the hashing and refuses the point addition: it is the
one every other package reads and carries no curve, so `tweakPoint` is injected
the way 23 injects `verifyAdvert`. A caller with none is told so rather than
handed a key nobody computed.

The tagged hashes are checked against `@noble/curves`'s own implementation of
the same construction, not only against themselves - a tree that agreed with
its own hash would agree with nothing else on the network.

### k and m are genesis, and the network ids moved

`arbitration_k = 5`, `arbitration_m = 7` joined the genesis parameters beside
`bond_maturity`: the leaf hashes them, so a round that disagreed about k would
compute a different output key for the same node and refuse a good bond.

Adding a field to a hashed object moves the hash, and it did:

  NETWORK_ID_REGTEST   14ba948f... -> a0115253aaeef3bb71a6bb4d12a6c5e2
                                      e7653010a6a015d371d1c905dda9e7e0
  NETWORK_ID_TESTNET4  0f50255b... -> 384dd0dd9750fd4db1accb308db6d5cd
                                      78d3da9974ef2f54bdba01a8bf70db8e

Recomputed by hand from the SAME public donation keys rather than by rerunning
`make-genesis.mjs`, which generates new keys every run. A network id that had
not moved would have meant the new fields were not in it.

### TWO PLACES 5A.3B's BYTES WOULD NOT EXECUTE, written as the spec writes them
### and named rather than quietly repaired

  1. Path A ends `... CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY DROP`, which leaves an EMPTY stack.
     A script ending empty fails. 5A.3B calls path A "the one to get right"
     because it is what returns the money if arbitration disappears - so this
     must be settled before a bond holds value, and not by a library
     reordering two opcodes on its own.
  2. Path B uses CHECKMULTISIG, which tapscript (BIP-342) removed; the
     tapscript spelling is CHECKSIGADD.

Neither affects this letter, which builds an output key and never spends one -
the leaves are hashed, not run. Both are recorded so whoever writes the spend
finds them named rather than discovering them with money in the output.

  D2 the arbitration keys not sorted            protocol red

  D4 the tree left out of the tweak             both red

## Item 24, slice 2: the leaves are programs that run

A leaf is not documentation. It is the program that moves the money, and its
hash is inside the output key - so hashing 5A.3B's own bytes would mean either
a bond that can never pay out, or an output key that has to change later and
invalidate every bond already posted. The whitepaper is intent, not a licence
to hash an unspendable script.

  path A  was  <node_key> CHECKSIGVERIFY <maturity> CLTV DROP
               ends on DROP with an EMPTY stack; Bitcoin needs a true left
          now  <maturity> CLTV DROP <node_key> CHECKSIG
  path B  was  <k> <keys> <m> CHECKMULTISIG
               tapscript removed CHECKMULTISIG (BIP-342): invalid on reveal
          now  <k1> CHECKSIG <k2> CHECKSIGADD ... <km> CHECKSIGADD <k> NUMEQUAL

### Measured by running them

A stack machine in `blwp-node/test/bond-spend.test.js` executes exactly the six
opcodes these leaves use. It is a FIXTURE, not a consensus engine: it can show
a program ends true for one witness and not another, which is the claim; it
cannot show Bitcoin accepts the transaction, and nothing claims it does.

  recovery, at maturity and after      spends
  the same witness one block early     refused, "the locktime 99 is before 100"
  a stranger's signature, any height   refused
  the SPEC'S OWN ORDER, same opcodes   refused - nothing left on the stack
  slash, five of seven                 spends
  four of seven                        refused
  six of seven                         refused - NUMEQUAL is a count, not a
                                       floor
  any other five                       spends
  five strangers                       refused

### The output key moved, which is the point

  before  2bc846cab3fdca04e588a7eeda4092d4047fac4ba83aa76451956a58f28cb6fe
  after   704bf508a57b0ec51898ee67a523184ff344025a6f80ff98dbfe4db210d2b4fd
  root    bcd94355... -> 4e8367dd...

Different leaf bytes are a different tree and therefore a different output key.
That is the reason to fix them NOW rather than after a bond exists.

THE NETWORK IDS DID NOT MOVE, and were checked rather than assumed: leaf bytes
are not genesis parameters. Both still equal the pinned values recomputed last

## Item 24, slice 3: the control block, and the parity that x-only throws away

Without a control block neither leaf is reachable: the output key hides the
tree, which is the point of taproot, so the tree has to be handed over at spend
time. A bond whose control block nobody could build is a bond nobody could
recover - and path A exists so that arbitration can never freeze one forever.

  shape        (leaf_version | parity) || internal_key || sibling = 65 bytes
  recovery     sibling is the slash leaf hash
  slash        sibling is the recovery leaf hash

THE PARITY IS INFORMATION THE 32 BYTES DO NOT CARRY. `lift_x` always returns
the EVEN point for an x-only key, so a spender that read the output off the
chain and lifted it would believe the parity is always 0. Measured over 40
bonds with random keys: 11 odd, 29 even. An assumed parity is a bond that
cannot be recovered a quarter of the time. So `bondOutputKey` asks the curve
for both halves and REFUSES a curve that answers with 32 bytes alone.

  re-derived from internal key + leaf + control block, on the real curve:
  both paths give back the output key on chain, parity included
  a block naming the wrong sibling gives back something else
  the right sibling under the wrong leaf gives back something else

`bondTapTree` now returns the internal key it was built with - a caller holding
the hashes and not the key could not prove a leaf belongs to anything.

  F2 the parity left out of the first byte            script red
  F3 a curve that never says even or odd is accepted  script red
  F4 the merkle path never walked                     script + key red
  F5 the internal key read as zeros                   script + key red

### One assertion removed for lying

A line in the real-curve test compared `built.parity` with itself through a
conditional - always true, proving nothing. Replaced with the fact it was meant
to state: `lift_x` of the output key is even, so the parity is extra
information and not derivable from what is on chain.

## Item 24, slice 4: the internal key is derived, not chosen

5A.3B makes the key path MuSig2(node_key, arbitration_aggregate_key), and it is
the path that moves the money without revealing anything - "a cooperative
release and a cooperative slash are the same transaction". The template ACCEPTED
thirty-two bytes for it, so whoever called it chose that path: a node could post
a bond whose cooperative spend is a key only it holds, and every check would
pass, because the key was an input to the check rather than a fact derived from
the keys the bond names. Census depth, committee size, bond floor, payout table
- the same fault, on the one path nobody would ever see.

### BIP-327 KeyAgg, coefficients here and the sum in the caller

  L    = H("KeyAgg list", pk1 || pk2 || ...)
  a_i  = H("KeyAgg coefficient", L || pk_i), and a_i = 1 for the SECOND
         distinct key - BIP-327's own optimisation, kept because an aggregate
         that skipped it would agree with no other MuSig2 implementation, and
         a key path nobody else can sign is a key path that does not exist
  Q    = sum a_i * P_i, done by the injected curve

Two steps, as the spec names two things: the arbitration keys aggregate to
`arbitration_aggregate_key`, and the internal key is the node's key aggregated
with that. Aggregation only - no session, no nonces, nothing signed.

  derived and reproducible          yes, and it is neither the node key nor
                                    the arbitration aggregate
  a different node key              a different key path
  a different arbitration set       a different key path
  a chosen internal key             refused: "not the MuSig2 aggregate of the
                                    node and arbitration keys"
  second key's coefficient          1, and the first's is not

### A BYPASS I HAD LEFT BESIDE THE DOOR

The check only ran when a caller passed the aggregate curve, so passing the
tweak curve ALONE still built a bond on any internal key. Both are now
required: anything that can add t*G can add a_i*P_i, so asking for both costs
a caller nothing and closes it. Found by an assertion I had written to say the
one-curve path was still served - reading it back made it obvious that it was
the hole, not a feature.

### The pinned output key moved once, and the root did not

  merkleRoot  4e8367dd... unchanged - the LEAVES did not move
  outputKey   704bf508... -> 9e0435f6... because the fixture stopped stuffing
              b32(0x22) as the internal key and started deriving it

The root is what pins the leaf programs; the output key under the stub curve
also depends on the internal key, so it moved when the fixture stopped
inventing one. Not a loosening: both are still pinned, and the reason is
written beside them.

## Item 24, slice 5: the arbitration set is the network's, and the door recomputes

### The set, as a genesis fact

The slash leaf hashes the arbitration keys, so a bond's output key is a
function of them - and a poster free to name their own would name themselves
and hold a bond nobody could ever slash. They are genesis now, beside
bond_maturity, arbitration_k and arbitration_m, sorted so a set is a set and
not an arrangement.

ON REGTEST AND TESTNET4 THE SECRETS ARE DERIVABLE BY ANYONE, deliberately:

    secret_i = taggedHash('BLWP/v1/TestArbitration', `${chain}:${i}`)

M2 distributes no money, and an arbitration set whose keys nobody holds could
never slash anything - a test network with an unusable set would be testing a
slash that cannot happen. Mainnet has no set here, exactly as it has no
BOND_MARKER: real keys held by real people are a decision, not a derivation.

The network ids moved again, recomputed by hand from the same public donation
keys - `make-genesis.mjs` was not rerun, since it generates new keys every run:

  NETWORK_ID_REGTEST   a0115253... -> b07c4a094718b9b28f6963f788838e02
                                      5a8ad591a7d7a498f0fe0ac0bdd14d9f
  NETWORK_ID_TESTNET4  384dd0dd... -> a677bbaed17223c848811410c07fb8db
                                      0fdaeda1e69821de717810fc8df17124

### The measurement that closes the letter's own question

A second node, holding only the published advertisement body and its own copy
of genesis - no fixture, no shared object, nothing the poster told it - rebuilds
the SAME output key, the same parity, and both 65-byte control blocks. A poster
naming its own seven keys produces a different output, and the rebuild says so.

### The door

`recognizeBond` given the set, the quorum, the maturity and a curve rebuilds
the key and compares it with the thirty-two bytes on chain, and its unchecked
list drops the script template. Given none of that it behaves exactly as
before and still lists it - nothing pretends.

  a bond built for one node key, presented for another   refused
  a bond whose maturity is 1 rather than the network's    refused
  a body naming template version 2                        refused by name

THE MATURITY WAS A NUMBER THE POSTER PICKED. Nothing held it to genesis, so a
node could post a bond already matured - withdrawable the moment it is posted,
at no risk, and counted by a census as though it were at stake. That is the
Sybil door 5A.3 exists to shut.

### The two small guards

`bondTapTree` refused nothing without a curve and would build a tree over any
thirty-two bytes; a tree is enough to produce a control block, so the guard on
`bondOutputKey` had a door beside it. It now requires the curve and the derived
key like everything else. And `bond_script_template_version` was written to the
wire, read back, and compared with nothing: version 1 is now bound to this
exact tree, so two nodes cannot read one number as two trees.

## Item 25, slice 1: the chain decides unspent and deep, not the entry

5A.2: a node is in the census "if and only if it has a bond output on Bitcoin,
CONFIRMED AND UNSPENT at census_height". RESOLVE re-applied that rule to the
entry's own `height` and `spent` - so whoever composed the list decided whether
a bond was live, on the single criterion the whole of eligibility rests on.
Re-applying a rule to a claimed fact is not verification. `commitCensus`'s own
comment even said the filters were "re-applied rather than trusted from
upstream"; the RULE was, the FACTS were not.

One reader now serves both paths: `chainFactsAt(blocks, censusHeight)`, pulled
out of SCAN unchanged, because two readers of one chain are two answers waiting
to differ. Nothing above census_height is looked at - 5A.2 makes the census a
pure function of the chain up to that height.

  a shallow bond whose entry claims an older height

  the same bond with an honest height, still too shallow
      excluded, "5 block(s) deep and this round asks for 6" - the claim is not
      quietly corrected either: a list that lies about the chain is a list to

      exactly today's behaviour, chainChecked false, and the gap named in

A fixture correction worth keeping: depth is measured from the TIP. The first
version put the tip ten blocks past the census, where nothing at or below the
census height can be under six confirmations - it would have proved nothing.
The tip now sits two blocks above it.

## Item 25, slice 2 step 1: the output at the outpoint, and a check that could not fail

Step 1 of the accepted sequence is to read the output at the claimed outpoint
from the chain rather than from the peer that resolved it. `chainFactsAt` now
records the output beside the height, so a caller has the script without going
back to the blocks.

BUT THE CHECK STEP 1 ASKS FOR CANNOT FAIL, and that is the finding. RESOLVE
already pins a resolved transaction to the entry's TXID, and a transaction with
that txid cannot carry different outputs - the txid IS the hash of them. A peer
swapping the output has to change the txid, and is then refused as "a different
transaction than the entry names".

So the check was written, measured, and REMOVED. Mutant L1 - the script taken
from the resolver instead of the chain - stayed green at 0 red, because the two
are the same bytes by construction. A check that can never fail is worse than
no check: it reads as verification and verifies nothing. The fact is recorded
where the reader is, and the test now pins the txid binding that does the work.

  /mnt/bitcoin/bitcoin-31.1/bin/bitcoind -datadir=/mnt/bitcoin       mainnet

Both running. Neither is regtest, and steps 2-4 need mining, a funded output
and a spend - impossible on testnet4 without coins and out of the question on

## Item 25, slice 2: a bond spends on a real node

### The oracle, and what it is not

This tree carries no BIP-341 vectors offline, so the only way to know a witness
is right is to hand it to a node. An isolated regtest bitcoind - own datadir
under the session scratch, port 19444, rpcport 19443, cookie auth, stopped when
the numbers were in - was that oracle. The two live nodes at /mnt/bitcoin
(mainnet) and /mnt/bitcoin/tn4 (testnet4) were not touched.

SO THE PINNED BYTES IN `test/bond-spend.test.js` ARE "WHAT BITCOIND ACCEPTED",
not "what BIP-341's own vectors say". Weaker about the code, stronger about the
result, and written into the test's own header so nobody reads it as the other
thing. `packages/blwp-node/tools/bond-regtest.mjs` re-runs the oracle.

### testmempoolaccept, every case

  recovery, honest, at maturity     allowed
  recovery, a stranger's signature  rejected: "Invalid Schnorr signature"
  recovery, one block early         rejected: "Locktime requirement not
                                    satisfied" - which is the whole reason CLTV
                                    is in that leaf
  slash, five of seven seats        allowed
  slash, four of seven              rejected: "Script evaluated without error
                                    but finished with a false/empty top stack
                                    element"
  a second node, from the body and
  genesis alone                     same leaf, same control block, same output
                                    key, and its own spend allowed
  after the honest recovery was
  broadcast and mined at height 109 chainFactsAt reads the outpoint as SPENT

### Two of my own probes were wrong, and the fixes are the point

  "same bytes"   two signatures over one message DIFFER: BIP-340 signing draws
                 auxiliary randomness. Byte-identity was the wrong claim. What
                 must match is everything the two nodes DERIVED - leaf, control
                 block, output key - and that the second spend is accepted.
  "spent?"       the census keys outpoints by the txid as it is HASHED, and an
                 API prints the reverse. The first check compared display order
                 against internal order and answered false about a spend that
                 had happened.

### What the sighash commits to, measured by moving each part

version, locktime, sequence, the output amount, the amount BEING SPENT, the
script being spent, and the leaf: each moves the sighash. The amount and script
of the input are taproot's own change, and they are why a signer cannot be lied
to about what it is signing away.

the census is unfindable in practice", one address per network. The census held

would have counted a bond posted on another chain. The two are different

                                      one that cannot say where to look for a

### Two vocabularies for one chain

`networkOf` answers 'testnet4' - the name genesis uses - and `bondMarker` took
only 'testnet', so the first honest wiring was told no marker had been chosen
for a network that has one. `networkAnchor` already accepted both. Both names
are answered at the source now rather than translated at a call site, which is
where a translation gets forgotten.

## Item 25, slice 4: a slash commits to the proof that justified it

A five-of-seven spend that pays a wallet address is not a slash. 5A.3B step 4:
"OP_RETURN = H(fraud_proof) || retrieval hint", and slash.js already fixes the
hash as the proof's own id - "because the slashing transaction commits to the
proof, every slash is permanently auditable".

THE MEASUREMENT THAT MATTERS IS THE ONE BITCOIND CANNOT MAKE:

  slash, five of seven, with the commitment
      bitcoind: allowed          protocol: commits to the proof
  slash, five of seven, no commitment
      bitcoind: ALLOWED          protocol: "that spend carries no proof
                                 commitment, so no slash it makes is auditable"

Consensus does not enforce step 4 - a spend with no OP_RETURN is a perfectly
valid transaction - which is exactly why the protocol has to. A bond taken with
no public record of why is the arbitration set's own offence.

And the rest still holds on the same run: honest recovery at maturity allowed,
one block early refused for the locktime, a stranger's Schnorr refused, four of
seven refused, a second node from body and genesis alone spending the same
leaf, and the outpoint read as spent after the recovery was mined.

The retrieval hint rides after the hash and its shape is not invented: the spec
fixes the hash and leaves the hint open, so bytes a caller appends come back
unchanged.

## Item 15, slice 1: SCAN finds its own candidates

Before: `scanCensus(view, { contract, candidates })` threw without a list. The
only way to a census root was to hand it the outpoints - so the census was a
function of whoever assembled that list, and 5A.4 step 1 ("scan the chain for
outputs paying the round's BOND_MARKER") was not code. 25.1's "discovery IS
chain state" held for the marker's construction and nothing read it back.

After: `candidates` is optional. Omitted, the scan walks every block at or
below `census_height` and takes a transaction only when all four hold - it pays
this round's network's marker, it carries a witness item that decodes to a
signed advertisement body, that body's `advertId` equals a 32-byte commitment
the transaction publishes, and the output the body names exists. A non-array is
still a throw: omitting means "ask the chain", handing something broken means a
caller built a list and got it wrong, and scanning instead would bury that.

  - THE MARKER'S NETWORK. Hardcoding 'regtest' left every test green, because

  - A VOUT THAT DOES NOT EXIST. Falling back to output 0 turns a body naming

    outpoint" - an outpoint the chain never had, named as if it did.

RETRACTED, not counted: "the scan reports the marker's value as bondSats".
It survived because it is a no-op - RESOLVE takes `output.valueSats` off the
funding transaction and overwrites the field before the floor is applied or a
leaf is hashed, so nothing ever read what the scan wrote there. The scan now
writes no amount at all, and the scan test asserts the field is absent, so a
number a later caller might trust cannot come back unnoticed.

## Item 15, slice 2: FILTER by the 24 template

Before: a census root could be taken with the 5A.3B template unchecked. The
template check is a point addition, `packages/protocol` carries no curve, so
`resolveCensus` ran without one and named the gap - "the bond script template
(no curve in this package)" in `unchecked` - and counted the entry anyway. That
is honest for a STEP and wrong for a CENSUS: a root taken that way is a census
over outputs nobody proved were bonds, and a stranger's taproot key is
thirty-two bytes like any other.

After: the COMPOSED census refuses. `deriveCensus` returns
`ok:false, why:"...template unchecked: regtest names an arbitration set and no
curve was injected"` unless the caller injects the set and both curve
operations. `resolveCensus` keeps its `unchecked` list - a step that says what
it did not check is honest, and that is now pinned as its own assertion.

Also in this slice, by ruling: a round that names no network is REFUSED, at
both doors. It used to fall back to `network || 'regtest'` in SCAN and to
`recognizeBond`'s own `network = 'regtest'` default in RESOLVE, so a contract
with no `networkId` was answered with regtest's marker on whatever chain it was
actually running.

And a set is this network's set or it is not a set: the arbitration keys, the
threshold and the maturity are compared against genesis before any entry is
judged, because a caller holding the wrong set would otherwise see every honest
bond excluded by name and read the chain as full of liars.

### Where the census tests live now

A root needs a curve, so the tests that take one moved to the package that has
one. `protocol/test/census-derive.test.js` and `census-chainview.test.js` are
now `blwp-node/test/`, on real secp keys and real bond output keys - the old
fixtures left the builder's 0x77 filler in place, which was invisible while
nothing recomputed it. Two composed-census tests moved out of
`protocol/test/bond-recognition.test.js` the same way; recognition itself
stayed, and needs no curve. `blwp-node/test/curve.js` is the shared injector.
`protocol/test/census-template.test.js` is new and holds the refusals, measured
where no curve exists. Nothing was dropped in the move: protocol 421 -> 400 and
blwp-node 122 -> 147 is 23 tests relocated plus 4 new refusal tests.

`commitCensus` deliberately does NOT carry this rule. It takes entries a caller
assembled and already believes about `advertId`; a template stamp checked there
would be a check on the caller's own word rather than on the chain. The

### Named remainders (not silent drops)

1. TREE-CARRIED COMMITMENTS, by ruling (Daniel, this letter). 5A.2 allows the
   advertisement commitment in "an OP_RETURN output of the funding transaction
   OR the taproot script tree". `commitmentsOf` reads OP_RETURN outputs only,
   so a tree-committed bond from another implementation is not a candidate and
   is dropped silently. This build produces and recognizes OP_RETURN only.
   Checking the tree form means recomputing the output key with a commitment
   leaf, so it needs the curve and belongs wherever that is wired.

2. `node_pubkey` CANNOT BE BOTH CURVES. Letter 23 verifies the advertisement
   signature as ed25519 under `node_pubkey` (`blwp-node/src/advert.js:88`);
   letter 24 feeds the same field into the secp256k1 taproot derivation as the
   node's key (`protocol/src/chain.js:307` and `:311`). An ed25519 public key
   is not a valid secp x-only point, so no real node can satisfy both at once.
   It is invisible today only because no fixture does both: the advert tests
   sign with ed25519 over a filler output key, and the census fixtures use secp
   keys whose signatures nobody verifies. Either the advertisement signature
   becomes BIP-340 on the same key, or the advertisement needs a separate bond
   key field. 5A.1 names no curve for the field, so this is a ruling, not a
   defect to pick a side on here.

3. No live bitcoind this slice, by ruling. Chain facts against real blocks are
   slice 3.

## Item 15, slice 3: chain facts against real blocks

Before: every census measurement in this tree ran on blocks a fixture composed
- the spend state, the depth and the height were all chosen by the test. A
fixture cannot lie about Bitcoin, which sounds like a virtue and is the
opposite: nothing had ever asked a real node whether these rules survive real
bytes.

After: `blwp-node/tools/census-regtest.mjs` posts four bonds on an isolated
regtest (own datadir under session scratch, port 29444, RPC 29443, cookie auth,
own wallet, stopped when the numbers were taken - it shares nothing with the
2-of-2 daemons or the mainnet/testnet4 nodes), spends one by a real 5-of-7
slash, leaves one two blocks under the census, marks one for another network,
and derives the census from the node's own blocks - header bytes included.

`protocol/src/block.js` is new: `splitBlock` turns `getblock <hash> 0` into the
view the census already takes. `parseTransaction` refuses leftover bytes on
purpose, so it cannot be pointed at the middle of a block; this walks the same
structure to find each span, and the span is handed back to `parseTransaction`
under that same rule. A wrong span cannot slip through - the slice fails to
parse, or its txid is wrong and the block's own merkle root refuses it. It sits
in its own module because the client bundles `tx.js` and never reads a block:
in `tx.js` it cost the client 2.4 KB of code nobody calls.

THE ADVERTISEMENT IN A REAL WITNESS. 5A.2 requires the body to travel in the
witness of the funding transaction, and the wallet cannot do that -
`sendtoaddress` builds its own transaction. Each bond is funded from a carrier
output whose one leaf is `OP_DROP <key> OP_CHECKSIG`, and the spend of that
carrier IS the funding transaction, with the signed body as the item the leaf
drops. Bitcoin's consensus rules accept it; its mempool policy does not
("bad-witness-nonstandard": a tapscript stack item that large is not relayed),
so the tool puts the transactions in blocks with `generateblock`, which
validates them fully without asking the mempool. Named, not smoothed over: a
deployment that posts a real bond needs a witness the mempool also relays, and
that is a construction question for the letter that does it.

### A defect the mutants found: depth was measured at the tip

`depth = tipHeight - height + 1`. Swapping it for `censusHeight` broke no test,
because every fixture had the two close enough together not to matter. They are
not the same rule. 5A.4 step 1 is "unspent AT CENSUS_HEIGHT with >=
census_confirmations depth", and the point of "given census_height, every
participant runs the same five steps" is that the answer cannot depend on when
it is asked. Measured against the tip it did: the shallow bond above is two
blocks under the census and seven under the tip, so a node deriving at the
census would exclude it and a node deriving five blocks later would count it -
two honest participants, two committees, which is the divergence 5A.2 exists to
remove. Fixed to `censusHeight - height + 1`, pinned in `census-scan.test.js`
across three tips, and the real-block fixture now has its tip past the census
so the two rules can be told apart at all.

## Item 18, slice 1: a ghost is produced, from the one door

Before: the GHOSTS frame existed and nothing made one. Measured at the start of
this slice - `encodeGhost` and `interestSet` had no caller anywhere in
`blwp-node/src` or `blwp-client/src`, so pieces 1 and 3 were a wire format and
a selection policy with nothing behind them. The frame could be CHECKED and
could not be MADE, and `ghostBinds` says out loud that checking is the smaller
half: "this cannot say the truck was AT x,z - only a replay says that".

After: `blwp-node/src/ghosts.js` builds a frame for one entry at one tick, and
the three truck words come out of `replay.js` - the daemon's only door to the
simulator - which now takes a `pictures` option and reads x, z and heading
inside the loop it was already running. `ghosts.js` itself never touches the
core, so the guard that counts the files reaching it still counts one.

A TICK CONVENTION, WRITTEN DOWN because the two ends have to agree: a picture
at tick N is the truck AFTER N was stepped. That is not the mark convention -
a mark names the state it REACHED, published after stepping N-1 - and the
difference is deliberate: 11's input chain covers TICKS, and `ghostBinds`
checks the tick against the inputs that cover it. The same state is mark N+1
and ghost N. `ghostForChecked` runs the checker over what it just built, so
drift between the two ends is a failing test rather than a frame a stranger
quietly rejects.

## Item 18, slice 2: spawn and subscribe are socket facts

Before: the `/play` socket was anonymous and had never pushed a byte. It took
input batches and answered a number, so the daemon had no way to address
anybody - a picture could be produced (slice 1) and delivered to nobody.

After: a connection says `watch <round> <entry>` and is thereafter shown the
others. On subscribing it is told `watching N` and then handed N frames - the
count first, so a client that reads it knows what is coming and no push
overtakes the answer to its own question. Every later batch that stores a tick
makes a new picture for whoever is watching that round.

The frames come from `Ghosts` (`src/ghosts.js`), which caches per round, entry
and tick, and whose every picture came out of `ghostFor` -> `replay.js`. The
selection is piece 3's `interestSet`, over positions that are REPLAYED rather
than announced: a mutant that fed it zeroed positions for anybody whose replay
failed dies.

### A hole in the client, found while checking consume

`blwp-client/src/client.js` matches EVERY socket message to the next queued
request in order. A pushed GHOSTS frame would be handed to whoever was waiting
for an answer - so a client that publishes inputs and watches ghosts on one
socket, which is the intended use, would read a picture as the answer to its
publish. The daemon side is right and the browser side cannot consume a push
yet. Not fixed here: slice 2 is socket facts by ruling. It is the next thing
18 needs, and it is `blwp-client`, not Unity.

## Item 18, slice 2b: the client consumes a push without stealing an answer

Before: `blwp-client/src/client.js` handed EVERY socket message to the next
queued request. The node had just learned to push GHOSTS frames, and one
socket carrying both is the intended use - a player publishes inputs and
watches competitors - so a frame arriving while a batch was in flight WAS the
answer to that batch. The client would read "the node stored N ticks" off 147
bytes of somebody's truck, the real answer would go to the next request, and
every answer after it would be one behind for the rest of the run.

After: the type byte decides. `TYPE_GHOST` goes to `takeGhost`, which decodes
it, counts it and hands it to `onGhost`; everything else - including a
RECEIPT, which is binary and IS a reply - keeps its place in the queue. The
client also gained `watch(round, entry)`, the one word that subscribes.

### The proof: red without the routing, green with it

Not "green after the fix". The same file, the same five tests, on both paths:

  routing removed (frames back on the queue)   0 passed, 5 failed
  routing in place                             5 passed, 0 failed

The assertion that fires on the unfixed path, in the test written for exactly
this window:

  a picture arriving while a request is in flight is not that request's answer
  -> AssertionError: a picture was handed back as the answer to a request:
     147 bytes

That test had to be built carefully. The end-to-end ones go red on the old
path too, but for the WEAKER reason - `said.shift()` drops a frame that
arrives with no request pending, so they fail with "the handler saw nothing".
The steal only happens while a request is genuinely in flight, and that window
is the node's to open, not something a test can win by timing. So the frame is
delivered the way the wire delivers one - a message event on the client's own
socket, carrying the bytes `node.ghosts.latest()` would have pushed - while a
`close` for a round this node does not hold is waiting for its answer. Nothing
inside the client is reached around; the injection point is the socket's own
event.

## Item 18 closed: two holes found on the way, and the numbers

The last check on this letter found two things on the spawn/subscribe/consume
path that nothing measured, and both are fixed rather than listed.

### 1. A subscription did not survive its socket

The node keys subscribers BY CONNECTION and `reconnect()` opens a new one. It
already re-did the two things a run needs - connect, and resume from the tick
it reached - and not the third. So a player who dropped for two seconds came
back publishing and BLIND: no error, no counter, the pictures simply stopped
for the rest of the run.

  before   node.watching() 1 -> drop -> 0 -> reconnect -> 0, no frames again
  after    1 -> 0 -> 1, and the next batch is a picture again

The client remembers what it asked to watch and asks again after resuming;
`rewatched` counts it, and a refusal is put on `error` rather than swallowed.

### 2. A stalled subscriber was buffered without limit

`showRound` sent to every open socket whatever its backlog. A 5 Hz picture of
a truck that has moved on is worth nothing by the time a stalled socket drains
to it, and the node holding it is unbounded memory for one slow player. Piece 2
already ruled the policy for the queue coming IN - "a full queue sheds pictures
oldest first and never evidence" - and this is the same rule going out, at the
same quarter of a megabyte the client uses to decide it is too far behind to
publish.

AND THE FIRST VERSION OF IT WAS WRONG, which the test written to pin the COUNT
is what caught. Marking shed frames as delivered lost a truck: a subscriber
who fell behind while somebody was driving, and that somebody then stopped,
never saw them at all - the picture was marked shown and never sent. There is
no queue to go stale here, because `setFor` recomputes the latest picture of
each truck every time, so a skipped frame is simply sent when the socket
drains and what goes out then is the newest one that exists. Counted, not
claimed.

  shed count   3 for two batches landing while behind: the first truck's
               picture dropped on both and the second's on one. A counter per
               STALL would say two, and could not show pressure at all.

  a subscriber that is behind is buffered rather than shed            killed
  a reconnect does not ask to be shown the others again               killed
  the client forgets what it asked to watch                           killed

## Item 26, slice 1: a short census is refused by name

Before: `census_min_nodes` was written into `network_id` by `genesis.js` and
read by NOTHING - not one file in any `src/`, not one test. It was not
harmless. `selectCommittee` ended in `scored.slice(0, slots)`, so a census with

round's `networkId`, and `meetsCensusMinimum(entries, contract, role)` answers
by name. `selectCommittee` asks it before it scores anybody and refuses rather
than slicing. A caller cannot name the minimum - not by an option and not by a
field on the contract - the same discipline the arbitration set needed in 24
and the confirmation depth in 25.

### Two gaps written down, not closed

1. PER ROLE, ONE FIELD. The spec writes `census_min_nodes per role`; this build
   carries a single `u16`. The one number is applied to EACH role separately,
   which is stricter than splitting it and moves no network id. Adding a second
   genesis field would change `network_id` for every network, so it is a
   ruling, not a fix to make in passing.

2. TESTNET4'S GENESIS SAYS 2, THE SPEC TABLE SAYS 3. Found while writing the
   tests: `genesisFor('testnet4')` carries `censusMinNodes: 2`,
   `gameVerifySlots: 2`, `settlementSlots: 2` - regtest's shape - where the
   three-networks table gives testnet 3 slots, threshold 2 and minimum census
   3. A value in genesis cannot be corrected in passing either: every parameter
   is committed in `network_id`, so changing one moves the network. The tests
   read the number off genesis rather than asserting 3, so they measure what
   rounds of this network are actually held against. Owner: whoever rules on
   testnet4's parameters before it carries a real round.

### The hole this letter still has

The census now decides who is SEATED, and nothing else. The node's own trust
still rests on `contract.nodes`: `verdict.js` counts signatures against that
list and `round.js` counts receipts against it, so a contract naming a
committee the chain does not support is still served. That is 26's own
sentence - independent nodes agreeing who is allowed into a round - and it is
named here rather than quietly left. It is not slice 3, and it touches letter
22's closed result path and the running 2-of-2 setup, so it needs a ruling
before code.

## Item 26, slice 3 step 1: one key - the node identity IS the bond key

Before: a node's identity was ed25519 while 5A.3B derives its bond output from
`node_pubkey` on secp256k1. Measured over 500 fresh identities:

  a valid secp x-only point   235/500 (by luck)
  and the secp secret held    0/500

So "the seated census is the trusted committee" was not a rule any node could
satisfy: the two lists could not hold the same bytes, whatever either said.

After, over 500 fresh identities:

  a valid secp x-only point   500/500
  can BIP-340 sign under it   500/500, secret in hand
  a bond can be built for it  500/500

Every signature a NODE makes is BIP-340 under that one key: its receipts
(`round.js`), its results (`verdict.js`, `verify.js`) and its advertisement
(`advert.js`). Letter 23's membership check is REPLACED, not weakened - a
receipt still has to verify, and a peer receipt signed ed25519 by a key that IS
on the committee is refused for the signature, while a well-signed stranger is
refused for the membership. The two refusals are pinned apart, so "the curve is
checked" is not proved by a test that never reached the curve.

THE PLAYER'S SESSION KEY IS UNTOUCHED. It signs marks, bonds nothing, and 26's
ruling is about `node_pubkey`; `round.js` still verifies a mark with ed25519
under the entry's session key, and the fixtures that check marks kept their
ed25519 verifier. Two of them had been swapped to BIP-340 by a blanket edit and
were put back - a verifier is chosen by WHAT it verifies, not by the file it
sits in.

### A rotation, named

A daemon that ran before this letter has an ed25519 pubkey in its identity row.
The SECRET is thirty-two bytes and works on either curve, so the published key
is recomputed from it and the row rewritten. That node's identity CHANGES:
receipts it issued under the old key verify under nothing. This is the honest
consequence of the two key spaces having been wrong, and it is not smoothed
over - the alternative is a node whose published key cannot sign.

### A defect the curve change exposed

BIP-340 is randomised. `takeReceipt` compared the whole SIGNED BYTES of a
stored receipt with an offered one, so one node signing one receipt twice -
which is what a re-send is - was called "has already receipted that
differently": an equivocation charge against a node that said the same thing
twice. It compares the BODY now. Equivocation is two different bodies; two
signatures over one body are two ways of saying it.

  a receipt signed on the old curve                      killed
  a peer's receipt signature not checked at all          killed
  two signatures over one body count as equivocation     killed
  an advertisement verified on the old curve             killed

## Item 27, slice 1: the seed a node seats with is the beacon's

Before: `selectCommittee` read `contract.committeeSeed` - thirty-two bytes the
round's AUTHOR wrote - so the lottery was a pure function of a value the
creator chose. THE GRIND, RUN RATHER THAN ASSERTED, on a fixed census of eight
bonded nodes with two slots:

  offline candidate seeds until a chosen pair was seated   34

Thirty-four. And since letter 26 made the seated set the only trusted list,
that pair is the whole committee - receipts, verdicts and all. 5A.11's
"committee cannot be overwritten" passes, because nothing is overwritten: it
is computed.

After: the seed is an argument the beacon fixes, and the field is not read.

  committee_seed = H(census_root_gv || census_root_settle
                     || round_id || round_randomness)      5A.5

`selectCommittee` refuses to draw without a 32-byte seed and never reaches for
the contract; `roster.seedFor` derives it from the network's randomness source
(`RANDOMNESS_SOURCE = 'bitcoin-block-hash'`) and refuses a round it has no
beacon for. No fallback: "I have no randomness" and "the committee is whatever
the contract says" must never be the same answer.

### The instruction changed shape, and here is the measurement that changed it

The letter's sequence said to COMPARE `contract.committeeSeed` against the
derived hash and refuse a mismatch. That check cannot be satisfied by any
honest round: `round_id` hashes the contract, so a contract carrying the seed
derived from its own id has no fixed point. Measured, six iterations, never
equal and never cycling - finding one would be a 2^256 search, not a
construction. And the spec agrees: §6's Round Contract carries
`randomness_rule`, `randomness_fallback`, `committee_time` and
`entry_open_time`, and NO committee seed. So the field stops being an input
rather than starting to be checked; removing the field itself moves every
round id and belongs with slice 2's field work.

                                 not decoration

  round's census height          when the round was made"
  no beacon at all               refused by name, no committee

## Item 27, slice 3: a round cannot open entries before its committee, or start without a window

5A.5's ladder, with the two rungs the contract already has times for:

  committee_time   beacon appears -> committees selected & verified
                   |  ENTRY WINDOW OPENS HERE
  start_time       round begins

  entry_open_time == committee_time
  start_time      >= committee_time + min_entry_window   (reference: 60 s)

`MIN_ENTRY_WINDOW_MS` is that reference, taken from the spec's own line rather
than chosen: 60000.

ENTRY_OPEN_TIME IS NOT A FIELD, AND MUST NOT BE. The spec's line is an
EQUALITY, so a second field could only disagree with `committee_time` - and
the reason is 23.1: the preimage shares are encrypted TO the settlement
committee, so an entry cannot be constructed before there is one. The equality
therefore holds by construction, and what is checked is the half that can be
got wrong: `Round#enter` refuses before `committee_time`, at the door, where a
client that draws no lobby cannot skip it.

## Item 27, slice 4: a fallback is the same beacon or it is nothing

Section 6 lists `randomness_fallback` beside the rule - "first block hash after
committee_time" - which on a network born reading `bitcoin-block-hash` IS the
rule. There is nothing else it could name, so the only honest values are
absent, empty, or the born rule itself. Anything else is a SECOND randomness
source, and a second source is a second committee: a creator free to fall back
would fall back to the beacon that seats their own nodes, which is 5A.5's whole
attack with an extra step.

  absent / null / empty / "bitcoin-block-hash"   accepted, and the seed is
                                                 unchanged - it is the same
                                                 beacon by construction
  "drand", "mock:7", "bitcoin-block-height",     refused: 'names randomness
  "BITCOIN-BLOCK-HASH"                           fallback "X" where regtest was
                                                 born reading
                                                 "bitcoin-block-hash" - a
                                                 fallback is the same beacon or
                                                 it is nothing', and no seed
                                                 comes back
  over the wire                                  impossible: the field does not
                                                 encode, so a decoded contract
                                                 carries none whatever the
                                                 sender wrote. The check is for
                                                 a contract OBJECT, the only
                                                 place one could still appear
  blwp-node                                      198 -> 199

THE FIELD IS NOT ENCODED, and that is the stronger answer rather than the
lazier one: encoding it would move every round id again and would CREATE the
channel the rule then has to close. A value that may only ever equal the born
rule carries no information, and the born rule is already on the contract.

### Mutants: 3 planted, 3 killed, 1 retracted

  a foreign fallback is accepted                       killed
  any non-empty fallback passes, whatever it names     killed
  an empty fallback is refused, so one must be named   killed

RETRACTED: "the fallback is checked against the contract's own rule, not
genesis". The rule check runs first and refuses any contract whose
`randomnessRule` is not the network's, so by the time the fallback is read the
two values are equal - the comparison is the same comparison. Genesis is what
the code names, because the network's born rule is the authority and the
contract's claim about it is not.

WHY THE FALLBACK IS NOT ENCODED, kept here so it is not read later as an
oversight: a value that may only ever equal the born rule carries no
information, the born rule is already on the contract, and encoding it would
move every round id again while OPENING the channel the check then closes. The
check guards a contract object, which is the only place a foreign fallback can
still appear.

PARKED, NOT MISSING: `published_at`. The grind fence is `committee_time` - the
first Bitcoin block after that instant - so "the creator did not publish after
seeing the beacon" is exactly as strong as that field and no stronger. 5A.5's
other half wants `committee_time >= published_at + min_publication_lead` and
five pre-randomness timestamp receipts, and this contract carries no
publication time. A later letter, by ruling, not a hole in 27.

Also by ruling and not by omission: `entry_open_time` stays off the contract
(5A.5 states it as an equality with `committee_time`, so a second field could
only disagree) and is enforced at the door instead; and there is no second
randomness source anywhere - no drand, no height fallback, no census_height
substitute.

## Item 27, the two rulings recorded

RANDOMNESS_FALLBACK STAYS UNENCODED (Daniel, accepted as the ruling): a field
that may only ever equal the born beacon carries no information; encoding it
would move every round id again and would OPEN the channel the check then
closes. Over the wire a foreign fallback is already impossible - the field does
not encode, so a decoded contract carries none whatever the sender wrote - and
the object-level check is the right place for the one case that remains. This
is a decision, not a slice of code waiting to be written.

PUBLISHED_AT IS AN M2 REMAINDER, now listed on PRIORITIES as item 30 rather
than living only here: 5A.5's other half asks for
`committee_time >= published_at + min_publication_lead` and five pre-randomness
timestamp receipts, and this contract carries no publication time. The grind
fence in place today is `committee_time` and is exactly as strong as that
field - no stronger, and it is not claimed to be. Not M3, not silent, and not
the next coding task: playable M2 is 28.
